articles.title: Alcolumbre acena a Lula e mira reeleição na presidência do Senado | G1
articles.standfirst: Aprovação integra agenda combinada com o governo antes da posse de um Senado mais à direita. Alcolumbre espera apoio para continuar no comando da Casa, mas também precisa fazer acenos ao bolsonarismo.
articles.summary: PEC da Segurança integra acenos de Alcolumbre ao governo em busca de apoio à reeleição no Senado. Ele também precisa dialogar com o bolsonarismo.
articles.body:
A aprovação da PEC da Segurança Pública foi uma vitória do governo Lula (PT), sem dúvida. Mas também foi uma vitória de Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP). Foi um combo de vitórias, e faz parte de uma agenda que foi combinada.

Desde a campanha eleitoral, temos falado aqui que o governo tinha pautas que avaliava que só conseguiria aprovar com esse Senado que está aí. Isso porque o Senado que saiu das urnas e toma posse em 2027 vai oferecer mais resistência às propostas do governo.

Sabendo disso, o governo colocou essa agenda para andar. Primeiro, o fim da escala 6 por 1, que passou e foi muito usado durante a eleição. Depois, a PEC da Segurança Pública.

A segurança já era uma promessa de campanha. A discussão sobre dividir o Ministério da Justiça e Segurança Pública, sobre as polícias e a integração vem de muito antes, ainda da transição de 2022.

Alcolumbre, quando recompôs a relação com o governo — ele estava rompido com Lula, é bom lembrar —, colocou-se à disposição para fazer essas pautas andarem.

Acabou a campanha para o presidente Lula e começou a campanha de Davi Alcolumbre para se manter no comando do Senado.

Os movimentos de Alcolumbre são acenos ao governo porque ele quer, em troca, o apoio para sua reeleição.

O Senado que saiu das urnas está mais à direita. Há nomes na base da direita e do bolsonarismo, como Rogério Marinho (PL-RN) e Tereza Cristina (PP-MS), na disputa. E Alcolumbre quer ser reeleito.

Com a vitória de Lula para a Presidência da República, ele avalia que o caminho ficará mais fácil, segundo interlocutores com quem tenho conversado.

Então, ele fez esses acenos e espera colher os votos no começo do ano que vem, quando haverá a eleição para a presidência da Casa. Só que também precisa fazer acenos ao bolsonarismo.

É por isso que falo em combo. Sabe aquela coisa de tentar agradar todo mundo? Vamos ver como ele vai sair dessa.

É sempre bom registrar quando o Congresso e os políticos tratam de temas de interesse da população, do dia a dia da sociedade. Segurança pública e violência urbana são preocupações presentes na vida das pessoas.

Mas o pano de fundo desses movimentos também é eleitoral. Agora, a disputa é pela presidência do Senado.

Presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e o presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP) — Foto: Ricardo Stuckert / PR

articles.title: Lula deve fazer pronunciamento no domingo, garantir que não haverá estelionato eleitoral e que fará ajuste fiscal | G1
articles.body:
O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) deve fazer um pronunciamento à nação no próximo domingo (8), no qual pretende prometer trabalhar pela pacificação do país, garantir que não haverá estelionato eleitoral e anunciar que fará um ajuste fiscal para cumprir as metas fiscais durante seu quarto mandato.

Segundo assessores presidenciais, Lula vai dizer que adotará medidas para garantir o cumprimento das metas de resultado primário ao longo do próximo mandato, preservando os programas sociais e cumprindo as promessas feitas durante a campanha eleitoral.

"Não haverá estelionato eleitoral. O presidente vai deixar isso claro, mas também vai dizer que seu governo terá responsabilidade fiscal durante todo o quarto mandato", disse reservadamente ao blog um assessor direto de Lula.

Outro auxiliar afirmou que a intenção é garantir a geração de superávits primários ao longo de todo o quarto mandato.

🔎 Estelionato eleitoral é uma expressão usada para definir casos em que um candidato, depois de eleito, adota medidas contrárias ao que prometeu durante a campanha. Apesar do nome, não é um crime previsto na legislação brasileira.

Lula já discute com os ministros Dario Durigan, da Fazenda , e Bruno Moretti, do Planejamento, medidas fiscais que o governo pretende aprovar ainda neste ano.

Durigan já entrou em contato com o presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), e com o presidente da Câmara dos Deputados, Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB), para agendar reuniões e negociar a aprovação das medidas.

Em seu pronunciamento, Lula também vai agradecer aos brasileiros pela reeleição, com destaque para mulheres, jovens e idosos, e dirá que vai trabalhar pela pacificação do país.

Interlocutores do presidente avaliam que Lula tem uma oportunidade para isolar politicamente a extrema direita, representada pelo bolsonarismo.

No terceiro mandato, ele já havia prometido enfrentar o avanço desse grupo político, mas, na avaliação desses interlocutores, não conseguiu cumprir esse objetivo.

articles.title: Cadu de Lula diz que PEC da Segurança vai facilitar integração entre forças federais, estaduais e municipais | G1
articles.standfirst: Governador eleito do RN elogiou aprovação da proposta e comentou o silêncio de Lula sobre dívida e juros. Em entrevista ao Em Ponto, da GloboNews, também abordou renovação do PT.
articles.summary: Governador eleito do RN elogiou aprovação da proposta e comentou o silêncio de Lula sobre dívida e juros. Em entrevista ao Em Ponto, da GloboNews, também abordou renovação do PT.
articles.body:
Governador eleito do Rio Grande do Norte, Cadu de Lula (PT), em entrevista ao jornal Em Ponto, da GloboNews — Foto: Reprodução

O governador eleito do Rio Grande do Norte, Cadu de Lula (PT), afirmou nesta quarta-feira (4) que a PEC da Segurança Pública vai facilitar a integração entre as forças federais, estaduais e municipais no combate ao crime organizado. A proposta foi aprovada pelo Senado em dois turnos na terça-feira (3) e segue para promulgação pelo Congresso Nacional .

“Ontem foi uma excelente notícia a aprovação da PEC da Segurança Pública, que vai ter impacto lá no Rio Grande do Norte”, afirmou, em entrevista ao jornal Em Ponto, da GloboNews.

Questionado sobre a ausência de manifestações de Lula a respeito de como enfrentar a dívida, os juros e o endividamento público e privado no próximo mandato, Cadu disse que o presidente pode estar usando esse tempo para consolidar ideias.

“E esse silêncio dele, talvez seja o tempo necessário, analisando como funciona a cabeça do presidente Lula, para quando ele se manifestar, ele já se manifestar em cima de ideias que vão estar consolidadas na cabeça dele para o rumo que ele vai dar para o país nos próximos anos.”

Ao defender a PEC da Segurança, Cadu afirmou que o avanço das organizações criminosas também atinge o Nordeste e defendeu o combate ao crime “com firmeza, com polícia na rua, com ocupação de territórios”.

Cadu também foi questionado sobre as diferenças entre a nova geração de dirigentes do PT e os quadros mais antigos do partido na condução da agenda econômica. Ele rejeitou a ideia de conflito e afirmou que as lideranças tradicionais contribuíram para a chegada dos novos nomes.

“Então, a gente não tem essa briga de gerações, vamos dizer assim", explicou. “É natural que agora, no quarto mandato do presidente Lula, algumas dessas lideranças ocupem espaços no governo do presidente Lula.”

Ao falar sobre a relação com a governadora Fátima Bezerra (PT), Cadu ressaltou sua lealdade à antecessora, mas afirmou que terá uma gestão com características próprias.

“Eu disse ao longo da campanha que eu tenho muita lealdade a Fátima, mas eu tenho um DNA próprio.”

Ex-secretário da Fazenda, ele disse ter uma trajetória mais voltada ao desenvolvimento e à geração de emprego e renda, enquanto destacou a atuação de Fátima no movimento sindical. “Então, o meu governo vai ser um governo diferente do dela. Eu acho que é isso, as ideias se complementam.”

articles.title: Rancho no TO coloca placa 'proibindo' entrada de petistas | G1
articles.standfirst: Proprietário afirma que aviso em propriedade de Lajeado, na região central do estado, foi colocado como brincadeira entre amigos. Especialista explica quando a restrição de acesso pode gerar questionamentos legais.
articles.summary: Proprietário afirma que aviso foi colocado como brincadeira entre amigos. Especialista explica quando a restrição de acesso pode gerar questionamentos legais.
articles.body:
Rancho fica em Lajeado, a cerca de 65 km de Palmas — Foto: Instagram/Rafael Magalhães

Uma placa instalada no portão de um rancho em Lajeado, a cerca de 65 km de Palmas, chamou a atenção nas redes sociais pelo conteúdo político: "Proibido a entrada de petista, inclusive parentes". O aviso faz referência a apoiadores do Partido dos Trabalhadores (PT) e estende a restrição até mesmo aos familiares.

📱 Clique aqui para seguir o canal do g1 TO no WhatsApp

O proprietário do Rancho 4 Marias, Rafael Magalhães, de 39 anos, afirmou que a placa foi colocada como uma brincadeira entre amigos. Segundo ele, o espaço é particular e não funciona como estabelecimento comercial.

“Eu coloquei no intuito de brincar com meus amigos que frequentam lá. Inclusive, um deles me ajudou a colar”, contou.

Rafael disse que recebeu a repercussão com tranquilidade e não viu problema nos comentários publicados sobre o aviso. "Democracia é tudo. A maioria dos comentários são de pessoas que não leram a publicação, mas tranquilo, entrei na brincadeira e até respondi alguns", afirmou.

A colocação da placa envolve o direito à propriedade privada e à liberdade de manifestação política, mas também levanta questionamentos sobre os limites desses direitos.

Segundo o advogado Gabriel Oliveira, especialista em Direito Civil e do Consumidor, a Constituição Federal garante o direito à propriedade e à liberdade de convicção política. No entanto, nenhum desses direitos é absoluto.

O advogado explica que é necessário diferenciar um imóvel particular, utilizado para lazer e recepção de convidados, de um estabelecimento comercial aberto ao público.

“Se estamos falando de um rancho exclusivamente particular, destinado ao uso pessoal e à recepção de convidados, existe maior espaço para o proprietário estabelecer critérios de acesso. Por outro lado, se o imóvel funciona como estabelecimento comercial, recebe clientes ou oferece serviços ao público, a situação pode ser diferente”, explicou.

Nesse segundo caso, a recusa de atendimento motivada exclusivamente pela orientação política do consumidor pode gerar questionamentos com base no Código de Defesa do Consumidor e nas regras de responsabilidade civil.

O advogado também ressalta que a simples instalação da placa não configura automaticamente o crime de discriminação previsto na Lei nº 7.716/1989, pois a opinião política não está expressamente entre os critérios discriminatórios criminalizados pela legislação.

Gabriel destaca ainda que a liberdade de manifestação política permite expressar oposição a partidos e defender convicções ideológicas. Esse direito, porém, não autoriza práticas que envolvam violência, ameaças, constrangimentos ou violações à honra e à dignidade de outras pessoas.

articles.title: Democratic socialist Janeese Lewis George elected mayor of Washington, D.C.
articles.summary: Democratic socialist Janeese Lewis George has been elected mayor of Washington, D.C., NBC News projects, continuing Democratic control over the capital city...
articles.body:
Democratic socialist Janeese Lewis George has been elected mayor of Washington, D.C., NBC News projects, continuing Democratic control over the capital city — but with a twist, as self-identified socialists make gains in cities across the U.S.

Lewis George will be Washington's first new mayor since 2015, succeeding Muriel Bowser, who did not seek re-election after three terms and is leaving public office. A large number of Democrats crowded into the primary in June for the right to be the party's shoo-in nominee in November. No Republicans ran.

Lewis George, a D.C. Council member, beat Robert L. Gross of the DC Statehood Green Party and independent Rhonda Hamilton for the seat.

Lewis George's ascension in Washington comes on the heels of other municipal successes for democratic socialists in recent years. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani is the highest-profile mayor who is part of the Democratic Socialists of America. Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson also identifies as a democratic socialist, though she is not a member of the DSA.

Lewis George will be responsible for managing the capital's relationship with the federal government and President Donald Trump, who posted after her Democratic primary win that he would not let Washington "be destroyed by a Communist adherent."

Lewis George said at the time: "The fact is that the mayor of our nation's capital and the administration are going to be meeting with each other. I'm willing to work with anyone, including the administration, to improve the lives of D.C. residents, and I will stand up to anyone who puts our city or its residents in harm's way. Making D.C. safe and more affordable for our residents is my immediate focus."

Lewis George has served on the D.C. Council since 2020, and during her campaign she championed universal childcare, expanding affordable housing and making city buses free for residents enrolled in SNAP benefits.

It was the first time the city has used ranked choice voting for its mayoral race, as it was approved as a ballot measure in 2024.

images.caption: D.C. Council member Janeese Lewis George. (Craig Hudson / The Washington Post via Getty)

articles.title: Alaska voters fear they might have voted for incorrect candidate
articles.summary: With two separate Dan Sullivans listed on Alaska’s Senate ballot, some voters expressed confusion leaving polling locations.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — With two separate Dan Sullivans listed on Alaska's Senate ballot, some voters expressed confusion leaving polling locations in the state.

In light of the DOJ's recent announcement that it will appeal the Alaska judge's dismissal of its lawsuit over the double ballot, NewsNation reporter Nancy Loo tracked down a "paranoid" Alaska voter over the weekend.

Alaska voter fears he picked the wrong Dan Sullivan

"I might be just having a brain freeze, but I don't remember the second Dan Sullivan. I definitely intended to vote for the real Dan Sullivan. I mean that was my intention, but for some reason, all of a sudden, I don't remember seeing the other," said the Anchorage resident.

He continued, "There is a slight possibility I voted for the wrong Dan Sullivan, but I mean … I'm hoping I'm just kind of getting paranoid, but I just don't remember. I don't remember seeing two Dan Sullivans without thinking about it."

Despite concerns, some voters say the ballot was "not confusing at all." NewsNation spoke with early voters at a polling place in Alaska who found the candidates clear on their ballot: "The way that they labeled everything on the ballot itself was very clear; you know who the incumbent was, you know who's not."

Democratic candidate Mary Peltola denies allegations that she influenced Dan J. Sullivan, speaking to a bar in Juneau, Alaska: "I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters."

Last week, NewsNation spoke with a former Republican U.S. House candidate who claimed a Democratic operative called him under an unknown phone number to convince him to run as an independent Senate candidate.

Mary Peltola denies ballot scheme, despite aide's claim

The allegation follows a New York Times report that Peltola's campaign worked with people trying to recruit Dan J. Sullivan to run for Senate in a "ballot composition project." The Times spoke with Peltola's former campaign manager and longtime aide, who was fired days before the Alaska primary in August and said the candidate was "definitely aware."

But is Dan J. Sullivan truly a fake candidate? The former teacher drew scrutiny as early as June , when the Alaska Division of Election determined Sullivan had not entered into the race as a Republican in "good faith," though the decision was ultimately overturned.

Back in Alaska , residents of the fishing community of Petersburg, where the candidate lives, say they haven't seen Sullivan in weeks. In recent days, the FBI has been visiting friends of the second Sullivan.

A Peltola voter from Petersburg told PBS that she believes Sullivan might not have run so honestly: "He probably viewed himself more as a spoiler than a legitimate long shot."

articles.title: Trump’s personal push of Darline Graham in South Carolina comes back to bite his party
articles.summary: In a stunning upset in typically reliably Republican South Carolina, CNN’s Decision Desk is projecting that Democrat Annie Andrews will defeat President Dona...
articles.body:
In a stunning upset in typically reliably Republican South Carolina, CNN's Decision Desk is projecting that Democrat Annie Andrews will defeat President Donald Trump's hand-picked candidate Sen. Darline Graham.

Andrews is flipping a seat Republicans have held for nearly three decades and a state that voted for Trump by nearly 18 percentage points in 2024. But the result has been building since Graham became the GOP nominee in late August.

Pushed by Trump, the governor appointed Darline Graham to finish her brother's term after his sudden death, and she decided to run for the full term. Graham eventually made it through a bruising special primary and runoff to become the GOP nominee after several personal interventions by Trump, including a rally in the state before the primary and dedicated spending from his PAC, MAGA Inc.

But the party didn't immediately unite behind Graham and her campaign struggled, needing help from outside groups. Concerns about her lack of experience persisted, especially after she said "national security is not my thing," during a primary runoff debate.

Andrews, a 45-year-old mother of three, launched her Senate campaign last year, acknowledging the uphill battle she faced running as a Democrat in South Carolina. She was originally running against GOP incumbent Sen. Lindsey Graham until he suddenly died in July.

The day after the GOP primary, Andrews was up with a statewide ad, "White Coat," introducing herself as "a mom to three kids and pediatrician" who will work with Republicans "to cut taxes and keep your family safe." She ticked off priorities like cutting healthcare costs and taking on insurance companies.

Like several other Southern Democrats this cycle, Andrews painted herself as an independent-minded moderate who is concerned about affordability, quality of life and corruption. The Democrat also tapped into lingering Republican frustrations with their candidate, calling Graham "unserious and unqualified" and noting the Senate race is "a job interview, not a coronation."

articles.title: Sen. Amy Klobuchar wins the Minnesota governor’s race, extending Democrats’ hold on the state
articles.summary: NBC News projects that Klobuchar has defeated GOP state House Speaker Lisa Demuth to become the first female governor in Minnesota’s history.
articles.body:
Sen. Amy Klobuchar has won the Minnesota governor's race, NBC News projects, a victory that will make her the first woman to lead the Midwestern state.

Klobuchar, 66, defeated Republican Lisa Demuth , the state House speaker, extending the Democratic Party's grip on the governor's mansion. Minnesota has not elected a Republican governor since 2006.

Although the national political environment favored Democrats this year, the party's brand in the state has been tarnished in recent years. Two-term Gov. Tim Walz, the Democratic vice presidential nominee in 2024, faced intense scrutiny over the state's handling of daycare fraud allegations.

Walz abandoned his bid for a third term in early January, later vowing he would "never run for an elected office again."

Klobuchar then jumped into the Democratic gubernatorial primary and went on to easily win the nomination. In launching her campaign for governor, Klobuchar pledged to be a bulwark against President Donald Trump, whose administration deployed federal immigration officers to Minnesota this year as part of a sweeping crackdown that some residents likened to an "invasion."

"Minnesota, we've been through a lot," Klobuchar said, referring to the fatal shootings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by U.S. immigration agents, as well as the assassinations last year of former state House Speaker Melissa Hortman and her husband.

"These times call for leaders who can stand up and not be rubber stamps for this administration but who are also willing to find common ground and fix things in our state," Klobuchar said. "These times call for grit and resilience."

She also nodded to the social services scandals that have roiled Minnesota, pledging to take a hard line against any abuse of public money.

"I will make sure the people who steal taxpayer money go to jail and root out the fraud by changing the way state government works," she said. "I will do my job without fear or favor. I've never shied away from taking on the powerful."

Klobuchar started her career in public office as Hennepin County's top prosecutor. She was elected to the U.S. Senate in 2006, making her the state's first woman to be elected to the chamber. She comfortably won re-election in 2012, 2018 and 2024.

Klobuchar also unsuccessfully sought the Democratic presidential nomination in 2020.

images.caption: Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn. (Heather Diehl / Getty)
Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth. (Ellen Schmidt / AP )

articles.title: North Carolina voters approve constitutional amendment requiring photo ID for mail-in ballots
articles.summary: North Carolinians are projected to approve a constitutional amendment requiring that all voters in the state show photo ID to cast a ballot, according to Dec...
articles.body:
North Carolinians are projected to approve a constitutional amendment requiring that all voters in the state show photo ID to cast a ballot, according to Decision Desk HQ.

The Require Photo Identification Amendment proposed changing the North Carolina Constitution to require all voters in the state to present an ID, regardless of whether they are casting a ballot in person or not.

The amendment's passage represents a win for state Republicans, who backed uniform rules for in-person voters and those who cast their ballot by mail.

It also marks a loss for the state Democratic Party, which cited concerns about the effects of a mail-in photo ID requirement on military members, students, rural residents and the elderly in advocating against the amendment.

North Carolina voters already have to show identification when they cast a ballot in person or by mail. The amendment's passage, however, enshrines the requirement in the state constitution, making it more difficult for future state lawmakers to overturn it.

Republicans in the North Carolina General Assembly approved the amendment's addition to this year's ballot in December 2024. Voters in North Carolina previously amended the state constitution in 2018 to require in-person voters to show photo ID at the polls.

images.caption: North Carolina voters approve constitutional amendment requiring photo ID for mail-in ballots

articles.title: Trump congratulates Democrats after dominant midterms, says he looks forward to working with them
articles.summary: President Donald Trump congratulated Democrats, saying he looked forward to working with them following a devastating Election Day for Republicans.
articles.body: President Donald Trump congratulated Democrats, saying he looked forward to working with them for the good of the United States following a difficult Election Day for Republicans. The Fox News Decision Desk projected a wave of Democratic victories, giving the party control of both the House and Senate. Trump warned earlier in the day that he would be quick to veto Democratic legislation if Republicans lost power, but struck a conciliatory tone when speaking to CBS News once results came in. "My message is congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country," Trump told CBS News late Tuesday. "Otherwise, I'd just veto everything, and they're not gonna want that." Trump previously made it clear he remained confident in his ability to pursue the MAGA agenda despite the outcome of the midterms. "I have the ultimate power — it's called 'veto,'" Trump previously told CBS News. During the earlier conversation, Trump suggested that his veto power could force Democrats to come to the bargaining table. "Historically, you veto for a couple of months, and then they come and say, 'We've got to make a deal,'" Trump said. "It's one of the stronger powers that a president has," Trump told "Special Report" anchor Bret Baier during live election-night coverage. "And they'll send over things that are insane, and I'll veto them. And after a couple of months of vetoes, they'll go out, and they'll say, 'How do we get this stuff done? articles.title: Democrats win Congress: How they did it, and what it means
articles.summary: With control of Congress, Democrats can challenge Trump’s agenda through subpoenas, confirmation votes.
articles.body:
The Democratic Party has pulled off a stunning upset in the United States midterm elections, flipping multiple bellwether seats to win comfortable control of the Senate and the House of Representatives.

The party’s total in the 100-seat Senate has now reached 54, with leads in two others. The Associated Press news agency also reported that the party had won the House of Representatives, marking the first time since Barack Obama’s second term that an incumbent president has had neither chamber of Congress with him.

With several races still too close to call, it could be several days before the final results are known, but several Democrats have already painted the outcome as a defeat for US President Donald Trump, who has himself conceded that his opponents bettered his party’s campaign.

We take a look at how the Democrats won control of the US Congress, and what they could do with that power.

The Democratic Party flipped several seats in the Senate, including many that it has not won in decades.

James Talarico, Texas: Trump had won the southern US state by 14 percentage points in 2024, and had endorsed Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general who has previously been indicted for fraud and was once impeached by the state legislature. But Talarico trounced him, leading by more than 11 percentage points with most votes counted. He is the first Democrat to win a statewide race in Texas in 32 years.

Adam Hamilton, Kansas: If Talarico did something no Democrat had accomplished since 1994, Hamilton went further: He beat Republican Roger Marshall, also endorsed by Trump, in Kansas, where the Democrats last won a Senate seat in 1932.

Josh Turek, Iowa: Trump carried Iowa by 14 percentage points in 2024. But Turek won this competitive Senate seat by 4 percentage points.

Annie Andrews, South Carolina: Another state that Trump won comfortably in 2024. This was a Senate seat that Trump ally and longtime senator, Lindsey Graham, held until his death earlier this year. Graham’s sister Darlene was appointed to fill in his seat until the election on Tuesday, and was strongly backed by Trump. It did not work. Andrews won by at least 4 percentage points.

Roy Cooper, North Carolina: Cooper did not just turn a previously Republican seat Democrat; he delivered a thumping win, beating Republican Mike Whatley by almost 20 percentage points.

Troy Jackson, Maine: Jackson turned over the previously Republican seat, defeating Susan Collins by almost 7 percentage points.

Sherrod Brown, Ohio: Brown won against Republican Jon Husted by almost 4 percentage points.

Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan: This was not a flip — the Democrats held the seat previously too — but El-Sayed won against Trump-backed Republican Mike Rogers to become the first Muslim senator in the US.

The Democrats have won the House, according to the AP, crossing the 218-seat mark needed for a majority in the 435-member chamber.

These wins include several seats that were previously held by the Republican Party.

With their victory in the House, hours after securing control of the Senate, the Democrats now control both chambers of Congress.

Democrats had promised to end the US-Israel war on Iran, bring down the cost of living and hold the Trump administration accountable for alleged abuses of power, if they won Congress. But following through on those promises may not be easy.

What powers would a Democrat-controlled Congress have?

The House and the Senate help pass laws and approve government spending. But neither chamber can act alone, and each has powers the other does not.

For instance, the Senate is uniquely empowered to approve Trump’s nominations to top government posts. With a majority in the Senate, Democrats can block the president from appointing allies as ambassadors, cabinet members and federal judges, including on the Supreme Court.

The party that holds the majority in the Senate also gets to control committees that can launch investigations, demand documents and summon witnesses to testify.

Separately, if a president or top government official is successfully impeached by the House, the Senate is then tasked with overseeing a trial that could result in the defendant’s removal from office.

Trump was impeached twice during his first term as president, in 2019 and 2021, but the Senate acquitted him on both occasions.

Commanding a Senate majority will also give Democrats greater power over legislation. Both chambers of Congress must pass a bill before a president can sign it into law.

There is a significant hurdle to the Democrats advancing their legislative agenda, though.

Even measures that have bipartisan support – like raising the minimum wage – would have to get past Trump’s veto. Trump has already signalled he plans to use the power liberally, telling a podcast on Monday, “I’ll veto everything.”

To override a veto, Democrats would need to rally a two-thirds majority in both chambers, meaning they would need some Republicans on their side.

Could a Democratic Congress hold Trump accountable?

Laura Blessing, a senior fellow at Georgetown University’s Government Affairs Institute, expects a Democrat-led Congress to actively wield its constitutional power to investigate.

“In terms of time spent and newspaper ink spilled, this is where you’re going to see the most action from Dems, by a mile,” she told Al Jazeera in an email.

Senator Richard Blumenthal is currently the ranking Democrat on the Senate’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations. He is expected to become its chair as a result of Tuesday’s vote.

In September, ahead of the elections, Blumenthal suggested to the Reuters news agency that Democrats would leverage their congressional majority to scrutinise Trump administration activities. “We will use our subpoena power, absolutely,” he said.

Congressional investigations, which do not require White House approval, could make life harder for Trump, whose family has spent the last two years expanding its business interests into everything from cryptocurrency and drones to artificial intelligence and prediction markets.

Trump’s personal wealth has soared by an estimated $2.2bn, according to financial disclosure forms released this year.

Democratic senators have already been laying the groundwork for such investigations. Some have sent letters to companies and government departments, demanding they preserve records.

Those requests have broached a range of subjects, including the private donations Trump solicited for his White House ballroom and accusations of partisan investigations.

Whether everyone will cooperate, however, is another question. Trump administration officials could challenge any future Senate subpoenas in court, potentially delaying investigations for months or years.

While Blessing does not expect “Trump’s nuclear family to show up to a subpoena”, she said there are many other witnesses Democrats could question, including government employees and people working for organisations linked to Trump’s inner circle.

That could help Democrats uncover potential wrongdoing involving Trump and his allies. But even if they do, there is no guarantee of legal consequences. Democrats could take evidence of a possible crime to prosecutors, but the Department of Justice under Trump would have to decide whether to pursue charges.

Impeachment is also a possibility if criminal action is uncovered, but no president has ever been removed from office as a result of such proceedings.

That has left some Democrats wondering how much time they should spend investigating Trump instead of focusing on issues that affect voters more directly.

“We just have to be thoughtful and strategic about where investigative work goes and not allow that to distract us from solving fairly immediate cost problems that American families feel,” Democratic Senator Sheldon Whitehouse told The Hill on Tuesday.

Could a Democratic Congress end the war on Iran?

The Democratic majority will not take control of the Senate until January 3.

That means the next two months may be critical for the US-Israel war on Iran, according to Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute of Responsible Statecraft, a foreign policy think tank.

Trump could respond to Tuesday’s midterm losses by escalating the war before Democrats have a chance to challenge him.

“He has shown a pattern in which, in the face of humiliation and defeat, he becomes more reckless,” Parsi said.

Once Democrats take power in the Senate, Parsi said, they would need to take an aggressive approach to rein in Trump’s war powers, including by trying to restrict funding for the conflict.

The Trump administration can continue spending money already allocated for military operations, but with control of Congress, Democrats could potentially stonewall any further funding for the war.

“It creates a limitation for how long he can pursue the war,” Parsi said. “If he needs more funding for it, we’re not talking about small sums that he can just reallocate from other places easily.”

Any budget bill, however, would need enough votes to overcome a possible Trump veto. There is also the question of whether Democrats would be willing to limit military spending.

Blessing noted that Democrats have historically been reluctant to withhold military funding out of fear of being accused of undermining US troops.

But there are other pathways Democrats could pursue to heighten pressure for the war to end.

They could, for example, use Senate control to investigate the war and whether the Trump administration complied with the rule of law in carrying out its attacks.

“Rigorous oversight would not restrict military operations by itself but could raise the political costs of the war beyond what the president or other key officials are willing to endure,” said David Janovsky, a policy analyst at the Project on Government Oversight, an independent watchdog.

It is unclear whether Democrats will unite behind a push to curtail the war.

But Parsi warned that if the party does not attempt to rein in Trump, its inaction could have political consequences.

“ It will no longer be just Trump’s war,” he said. “They will also co-own it, because they will be complicit, because they have the ability to stop it.”

Could a Democratic Senate bring down the cost of living?

Ahead of the midterm elections, voters consistently ranked economic issues as a top concern.

Dean Baker, an economist and cofounder of the Center for Economic and Policy Research think tank, said one of the biggest things Democrats could do to relieve such concerns is push for an end to the war on Iran.

Since the war began in February, Iran has restricted commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital artery for the global fuel and fertiliser trade.

Using the Senate to scrutinise the administration’s handling of the war could help build political pressure to end it. That, in turn, could bring down petrol prices and ease pressure on household budgets, Baker argued.

Democrats could also try to bring down healthcare costs.

The expiration of enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies in 2025 has left many Americans facing higher insurance premiums. Democrats could try to restore those subsidies, along with reversing cuts to Medicaid, the government healthcare programme for low-income Americans.

Baker said they could use negotiations over government spending to push Republicans to agree to such measures. With bipartisan support and widespread public backing, it would be politically difficult for Trump to refuse any effort to reduce healthcare costs.

“They can make the politics such that he doesn’t want to veto it,” Baker said of the Democrats.

Democrats could also try to reverse Trump’s tariffs, although that would require support from the House and either Trump’s approval or enough votes to override his veto.

But even if they succeeded, prices would not fall overnight.

“Prices are like rockets and feathers. They shoot up like rockets; they come down like feathers,” said Alex Jacquez, chief of policy and advocacy at Groundwork Collaborative, a progressive economic think tank.

But there is another way Democrats could try to tackle high prices, without needing Trump’s approval.

With control of Senate committees, they could investigate companies over everything from grocery prices and rents to rising electricity bills.

“There’s a lot of precedent for getting some real material outcomes just through having the gavels and being able to subpoena CEOs and haul people in front of Congress,” Jacquez told Al Jazeera.

articles.title: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan’s high-stakes Senate race
articles.summary: NBC News projects that El-Sayed, a progressive former public health official, has defeated Republican Mike Rogers, a key victory for Democrats.
articles.body: Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and former public health official aligned with the Democratic Party’s left flank, has won Michigan’s highly hostile Senate race, defeating his Republican rival, former Rep. Mike Rogers, NBC News projects. El-Sayed, 42, overcame a raft of Islamophobia fomented by President Donald Trump and others to become the first Muslim elected to the chamber. He also overcame a last-minute defection from Rep. Haley Stevens, a vanquished primary rival who reneged on her pledge to support him and endorsed Rogers after she attended church with him Sunday. Follow live updates on the midterm elections “They tried to confuse you, so let me just set the record straight,” El-Sayed told supporters early Wednesday. “I love America” El-Sayed also had sharp words for those who had made an issue of his religion, from Rogers on up to Trump. He said he relished that it would be Vice President JD Vance, with whom he has tangled publicly, who swears him into the Senate. “So Mike, enjoy your retirement,” said El-Sayed, referring to Rogers. “See, you chose hate, and Michigan chose hope. May we never have to see the likes of you in this state again.” El-Sayed’s victory extends a long-running GOP drought in the state. A Republican has not won a Senate seat in Michigan since 1994. El-Sayed will succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters. The clash between El-Sayed and Rogers, 63, was rated among the country’s most closely watched and aggressively fought, given El-Sayed’s alliance with progressive firebrands such as Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. El-Sayed’s criticism of the Israeli government, which he has accused of genocide, was also a consistent flash point. A group affiliated with the pro-Israel group AIPAC spent more than $30 million in an unsuccessful effort to lift Stevens over El-Sayed in the Democratic primary and re-engaged in Michigan in the closing weeks of the general election. Stevens, meanwhile, linked her defection from El-Sayed to his position on Israel and his campaign’s suggestion that she was not welcome at his campaign events after she began voicing her criticism more in the race’s closing days. Rogers and his Republican allies tried to spin El-Sayed’s anti-Israel stance into attacks that evoked his religion and raised questions about his loyalties. Vance, in particular, routinely attacked El-Sayed — a rift that grew out of El-Sayed’s sarcastic questioning of whether Vance’s late, white Appalachian-born grandfather would have approved of his Indian American wife. Trump’s attacks on El-Sayed’s faith went furthest. Within days of El-Sayed’s August primary victory, Trump began falsely asserting that “jihadists” were gaining purchase in U.S. politics and government. The attacks escalated over the next three months, with Trump at one point whipping a crowd in Youngstown, Ohio, into a frenzied chant of “Deport! Deport!” He often referred to El-Sayed by his middle name, Mohamed. El-Sayed had a handy retort for that one. “That’ll be Sen. Mohamed to you, bro,” he said at an Oct. 25 event with Sanders. Trump’s rally the same day in Port Huron, Michigan, brought an escalation in his rhetoric. “I’m here to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator, and that’s the fact,” Trump said. “We’re not going to let that happen.” Rogers tried to distance himself from the most heated rhetoric, but he also accused El-Sayed of harboring ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, an international Sunni Islamist organization founded in Egypt in 1928. The Trump administration has designated certain chapters of the group as terrorist organizations. El-Sayed has denounced and denied having any ties to the group. El-Sayed framed his campaign pitch around a simple, ideologically focused slogan: “Money out of politics, money in your pockets and Medicare for All.” While that established him firmly to the left of his party, polling throughout the race suggested his message was helping him make strides with Trump voters. Rogers struggled to escape Trump’s shadow. In the race’s closing weeks, he tried to distance himself from Trump’s war in Iran and tariffs — two developments that caused prices to rise and compounded voters’ economic concerns. “Well, there are some things that Canada does that [are] absolutely unfair to Michiganders and the rest of the country,” Rogers said in an interview this month with “NBC Nightly News.” “I’ve been a targeted and temporary tariff guy to correct those things. I thought the broad sweep was too much, and I’d like to see it wrapped up.” Asked in the interview whether the Iran war was a mistake, Rogers replied less than confidently: “Well, we’ll find out. I don’t think so.”

articles.title: Thune plans to run for Republican minority leader after Dems' midterm takeover
articles.summary: John Thune intends to run for Senate minority leader after Republicans lost at least five seats in the 2026 midterm elections, a source says.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: A source close to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told Fox News Digital that the South Dakota Republican intends to run for Senate minority leader following the GOP's sweeping defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections. Thune is expected to seek the leadership position despite Republicans losing at least five seats in the upper chamber, including contests in traditionally Republican strongholds such as South Carolina and Texas. The losses came amid declining approval ratings for President Donald Trump, whose administration faced criticism over the war in Iran, immigration enforcement operations and high gas prices in the months leading up to the election. CONSERVATIVES STUNNED BY 'CATASTROPHIC' MIDTERM BLUE TSUNAMI, BLAME TRUMP'S IRAN WAR, HIGH GAS PRICES Following the defeat — which saw the Senate margins not only flip but also widen — Thune defended Senate Republicans' legislative record over the past two years. The GOP conference has "put up a strong record of accomplishment that's created safer streets, more money in Americans' pockets, and new opportunities for families and businesses to get ahead," Thune wrote on social media. TRUMP KEEPS CALLING THUNE DESPITE PUBLIC FIGHT OVER SAVE AMERICA ACT The majority leader also highlighted Republicans' efforts to advance Trump's legislative and judicial priorities despite Democratic opposition. "After fighting Democrat obstruction at every turn, we prevented the largest tax hike in American history, secured our border in an unprecedented way, confirmed the president's Cabinet at the fastest pace in two decades, and put strong conservative judges on benches across the country faster than we have since the Reagan administration," Thune wrote. TRUMP'S PATIENCE 'RUNNING OUT' AS THUNE FIRES BACK OVER STALLED ELECTION SECURITY BILL Earlier this year, Thune also faced criticism from Trump and House Republicans over the Senate's failure to advance key legislation championed by the president, including the SAVE America Act. The election integrity legislation passed the House of Representatives three times in 2026 but stalled in the Senate, where the chamber's 60-vote threshold to overcome a filibuster prevented Republicans from advancing the measure. REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: CONGRESS BRACES FOR POST-ELECTION GAME OF MUSICAL CHAIRS AS LEADERSHIP BATTLES LOOM It remains unclear whether Thune will face a challenger for the Senate Republican leadership position. Another source close to the Republican majority in the Senate told Fox News Digital that Thune's ambition might land him serious backlash, adding that the conference did not deliver on key promises of the president's agenda which could have hurt Republican voter turnout in the midterm elections. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The source pointed to the fact that the upper chamber was only in session for 217 days in 2025, and 148 in 2026, as a reason for record-low approval of the chamber ratings among Republican voters that hurt voter turnout on Tuesday. The source hinted that outspoken allies of the president in the chamber, such as Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, could emerge as good alternatives.

articles.title: These candidates made history in the 2026 midterm elections
articles.summary: Tuesday's election saw an expansion of representation among America's lawmakers.
articles.body:
The 2026 midterm elections made history for several candidates, as voters are projected to have elected the country's first Black, Native American and Latina female governors and more major firsts.

All eyes were on the results Tuesday night in the high-stakes election, in which House and Senate races will determine the balance of power in Congress.

But the midterms have also seen an expansion of representation among America's lawmakers, with several candidates celebrating groundbreaking wins.

This story will be updated as more wins are projected.

Democratic candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms is projected by ABC News to become the next governor of Georgia -- beating billionaire Rick Jackson in the closely watched race.

The projected win for Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, flips the Georgia governor's mansion blue in a state that President Donald Trump won in 2024.

In the closing stretch of the race, Bottoms often repeated on the campaign trail that Jackson "may have the money, but the people still have the power." Before the end of the cycle, Jackson had spent more than $200 million of his personal fortune on his campaign.

Georgia hasn't elected a Democrat for governor since 1998. The seat is currently held by Republican Gov. Brian Kemp, who was term-limited this year.

This is a major win for Georgia Democrats, who have targeted this seat for years, falling short in 2018 and 2022 with Democrat Stacey Abrams. In 2018, Abrams lost to Kemp by a 1.4-point margin.

Deb Haaland, the former U.S. Secretary of the Interior, is projected to win New Mexico's gubernatorial race, becoming the first indigenous governor in U.S. history.

"Thank you, New Mexico! It is the honor of my lifetime to be elected your 33rd Governor," Haaland wrote on X. "Tonight, you made history. You chose a future where New Mexico comes first, where working families have a chance to get ahead, and where every New Mexican has a voice."

She is a member of the Laguna Pueblo, a federally recognized tribe in the state.

Haaland's projected win on Tuesday was against former Rio Rancho Mayor Gregg Hull.

In 2018, Haaland became one of the first two Native women elected to Congress.

"In 230 years, there's never been a Native American woman in Congress. I have never seen myself in that body of our government," Haaland said in an interview with ABC News at the time.

The Texas gubernatorial race is also projected to see a historic first, with Democratic Rep. Gina Hinojosa becoming the state's first Latina governor.

Hinojosa was running against Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who was aiming to win his fourth term.

The stunning projected win for Hinojosa, who served in the Texas state House, comes after running on education reform and criticizing Abbott over AI data centers.

"This is our last best chance to take back Texas for the people," she wrote on X ahead of the election.

ABC News can project that Democrat Dr. Abdul El-Sayed will win his Senate election against his Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers.

He will make history as this country's first-ever Muslim Senator. He faced consistent Islamophobic attacks from top Republicans, including the president.

El-Sayed consistently led in the polls, but faced a late challenge with Rep. Haley Steven's endorsement of Rogers on Sunday, but was able to rally the party around him in the closing days. His campaign focused on issues like Medicare for all and campaign finance reform.

Republican Rep. Byron Donalds is projected by ABC News to win the gubernatorial race in Florida, becoming the state's first Black governor.

"I am humbled and grateful beyond measure," Donalds said in a victory statement posted to X. "As your Governor, I will give you everything I have. We are going to make life in Florida more affordable. We are going to keep our streets safe. We are going to invest in our young people so that they can attain the Florida Dream that all of us love so dearly."

His campaign made headlines in September when Donalds' website was updated to remove some prominent references to Trump. According to the Miami Herald, Donalds removed at least eight references to Trump from his website.

Shortly after the changes, however, Donalds posted a statement on X touting his endorsement of the president.

"I am proud to have President Trump's endorsement. While everyone is focused on our website, check out our policy proposals to make life more affordable for Floridians," Donalds wrote at the time.

Dr. Amy Acton, the former director of the Ohio Department of Health, is projected to defeat GOP opponent Vivek Ramaswamy for the Ohio governor's seat.

Acton will become the first woman elected governor in Ohio and the first Jewish governor in the state's history.

The defining moment of this campaign came with an ad made by the Ramaswamy campaign that tried to use Acton's estranged mother, who fled the state with a husband who was indicted for raping Acton as a child, to call Acton a liar. The ad prompted major backlash and an influx of support and visibility for Acton.

In battleground Wisconsin, Democrat David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, will win and become the state's first Black governor, ABC News projects.

Crowley defeated Tom Tiffany, a Trump ally, for the open seat to succeed outgoing Democratic Gov. Tony Evers. A former state lawmaker, Crowley campaigned on his background running the state's largest county and fended off attacks from his Republican opponent, who cast him as weak on crime and immigration.

Crowley campaigned on reducing the cost of living and rejecting "MAGA extremism."

"Thank you, Wisconsin. Thank you for believing in me," he wrote in a statement on X Tuesday night. "Serving as your governor will be the honor of a lifetime."

Democrats pinned their hopes on Crowley to win a state government trifecta for the first time in over a decade in the swing state.

In New Hampshire, ABC News projects that U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas will win the Senate race, becoming the first openly gay senator.

He is projected to beat former Sen. John Sununu, a Republican backed by President Donald Trump, in the race that was seen as a must-hold for the Democrats.

Pappas campaigned with major Democratic figures such as former Vice President Kamala Harris and California Gov. Gavin Newsom.

articles.title: STATE OF PLAY: Blue wave sweeps Democrats into power, with key races still hanging in balance
articles.summary: Democrats flipped GOP seats in Texas, Ohio, Iowa, North and South Carolina as a blue tsunami swept midterm elections far beyond expectations.
articles.body: Democrats decisively recaptured majorities in the House and Senate in the midterm elections, riding a massive blue wave that exceeded expectations. But with Tuesday turning into Wednesday and a handful of high-profile races still to be called, the big question remaining is whether the already formidable Democratic congressional majorities keep growing. In the battle for the Senate, Democrats stormed to the majority by flipping GOP-held seats in Maine, Ohio, Kansas, Iowa, Texas, North Carolina and South Carolina, while successfully defending open seats in Michigan and New Hampshire. HEAD HERE FOR FOX NEWS LIVE UPDATES ON THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS Meanwhile, Senate races for two GOP-held seats were still too close to call. In Mississippi, Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democratic challenger Scott Colom appeared deadlocked. In Alaska, GOP incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan had a slight edge over former Rep. Mary Peltola with votes still being counted. In the battle for the House, thanks to the stunning blue tsunami, Democrats easily cleared the 218-seat threshold needed to recapture the chamber. CLICK HERE FOR THE LATEST MIDTERM ELECTION RESULTS AS THE VOTES CONTINUE TO BE COUNTED But with plenty of races still outstanding, the big question is just how large of a majority will Democrats end up with when all the votes are counted. As of early Wednesday, Democrats had won 228 seats to 139 for the GOP, with 68 races yet to be called. In gubernatorial showdowns, competitive races in Alaska and Kansas had yet to be called. The results amounted to a stunning rebuke of President Donald Trump and the GOP. "The American people reduced the red brick wall to a pile of bricks," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., told reporters. And looking ahead to January, when the new Congress gets to work, Schumer said, "We have five words for the American people. Relief is on the way." But Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said, "As we head into 2027, Senate Republicans will not stand idly by as the far-left, socialist wing of the Democratic Party attempts to unwind everything we’ve done." Thune said that Senate Republicans will work with Trump "to stop the worst impulses of Democrat extremism. We cannot let their fringe positions become the mainstream." CHECK OUT THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB Trump spent the past two months repeatedly stressing to supporters to "pretend I’m on the ballot," as he tried to energize the Republican base. But, as the results were pouring in on Tuesday night, the president took to social media to argue, "I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!" CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Minutes later, the president, in an interview on Fox News with anchors Bret Baier and Martha MacCallum, complimented the opposition party, saying, "I think the Democrats did a good job." And pointing to their incoming congressional majorities, Trump added, "I can work with them on many things."

articles.title: Elon Musk jokes about GOP election defeat after spending record sums on party
articles.summary: Tech billionaire Elon Musk joked on Wednesday about Republicans' defeat in US midterm elections after spending hundreds of millions of dollars to help the pa...
articles.body:
Tech billionaire Elon Musk joked on Wednesday about Republicans' defeat in US midterm elections after spending hundreds of millions of dollars to help the party.

Democrats seized control of the US Congress on Tuesday, capturing both the Senate and House of Representatives in a stunning rejection of President Donald Trump's political agenda.

"Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time," Musk said on X, including the shrug emoji.

Musk contributed nearly half a billion dollars to Republican political efforts, making him the largest individual contributor in a federal election cycle since unlimited election spending was allowed in 2010, according to campaign finance tracker OpenSecrets.

His donations have mostly gone to his Republican-leaning America PAC, as well as to the Republican Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) super PAC.

The SLF used Musk's $158 million in donations in September to support Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate candidate in Texas.

The Texas Senate election topped the list in terms of expenditure, with Paxton's Democrat challenger James Talarico facing more than $200 million in opposition from outside spending groups.

Talarico defeated Paxton, a close ally of Trump, to become the first Democrat to win statewide office in Texas since 1994.

He took aim at Musk at a victory rally in Austin.

"In this race, we went up against our own Goliaths. The richest man in the world, the most powerful man in the world and the entire Washington, DC establishment," Talarico said.

He also targeted billionaires "who own the social media algorithms, who own the cable news networks, who own the politicians fighting on our screens" and who "want us at each other's throats."

Democrat Gina Hinojosa unseated incumbent Texas Governor Greg Abbott in another blow to the deeply conservative southern border state.

Hinojosa said she asked at the start of her campaign if Texas was "a state that is by and for the people of Texas."

"Or is this the billionaire's world and we just live here? Does Texas belong to the parents and their children? Or the billionaires trying to dismantle our schools? Does Texas belong to the farmers and ranchers who have worked this land for generations? Or the corporations trying to buy it up?" she said after her victory.

Talarico and Hinojosa both campaigned on tighter regulations for AI data centers.

The spread of data centers across Texas has become a central issue as residents worry about rising electricity bills, water use and strain on the power grid.

Musk has moved the headquarters of his comapanies Tesla, SpaceX and X to Texas.

"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk joked on X after the result.

The Supreme Court ruled in 2010 that the government cannot limit political spending by corporations, unions and other groups if they spend it independently of candidates.

A lower court decision ruled that these organizations could also raise an unlimited amount of money from donors.

Now, big donors can allocate vast sums of money to try to influence elections and remain anonymous by donating through secondary organizations.

Spending sprees by donors have surged under Trump's administration, with Musk's large donations encapsulating the new reality of pay-to-play politics.

articles.title: Trump told voters, 'Pretend I'm on the ballot.' They did.
articles.summary: President Donald Trump spent two months urging Americans to pretend he was on the ballot. On Tuesday, they did just that. Voters delivered a stunning rebuke...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump spent two months urging Americans to pretend he was on the ballot. On Tuesday, they did just that.

Voters delivered a stunning rebuke to Trump's party that rivaled anything Republicans had suffered in 50 years, defeats on ruby-red turf that Trump won handily just two years ago, where he has dominated politics for nearly a decade and against candidates he had in some cases handpicked.

Not only did Democrats flip Senate and governor seats in red states, but at times by eye-popping margins.

"The message is very clear and very simple here. It was a complete repudiation of the party as defined by Donald Trump," said Mike Murphy, a Los Angeles-based Republican consultant who worked for candidates in the pre-Trump GOP, including Jeb Bush and John McCain.

"We have a little saying in show business, 'box office poison,' and that's what Donald Trump has become."

More than 41 times in recent weeks, The Washington Post found, Trump told voters to act this November as if the midterms were a referendum on him - a bold dare for a president whose approval ratings had reached historic lows as a growing number of Americans reported opposing his policies and his behavior in office.

In just two years since Trump's remarkable presidential victory campaign, in which he vowed to lower consumer prices, he has generated deep resentment of his policies. Voters blamed his decision to go to war against Iran and his tariff policies for raising prices, instead.

Trump left himself no hedge against being held responsible for voter unhappiness because he had molded the GOP into his image over the last decade. He demanded complete loyalty from Republicans and sought to cast out those who opposed him. Then he made himself the face of the party's midterm messaging, not only calling for his advisers to feature him in midterm television advertisements but demanding that the GOP host a first-of-its-kind midterm convention to tout his policies.

Trump "brought a Chernobyl-level disaster to the Republican Party," Murphy said, "the worst beating the party has taken since '74, after Watergate."

That year, Democrats gained 49 seats in the House and four in the Senate, on the heels of newly installed President Gerald Ford's pardon of Richard M. Nixon and amid a spike in gas prices and overall inflation.

So far this year, with some races left to be called, Democrats have flipped seven Senate seats and at least 25 in a House with far fewer competitive seats. They also flipped several governorships and state legislative chambers.

In Texas on Tuesday, James Talarico's double-digit lead over Trump's chosen Senate candidate Ken Paxton was particularly symbolic, taking place in a state long seen as the heartland of the conservative movement.

In North Carolina, a state Trump won three times, Democrat Roy Cooper not only flipped a Senate seat but was leading early Wednesday by nearly 20 percentage points. Democrats snatched Senate seats in other deeply red states, including South Carolina and Kansas.

In Pennsylvania, the swing state that sealed Trump's comeback victory, Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro was winning reelection by 22 points with nearly all the vote counted.

For months, Trump's advisers insisted that he was the key to Republicans' being able to defy poor expectations in the midterms. Trump, they argued, could rally Republicans to the polls like no other and was responsible for assembling a coalition that included young and diverse voters that the GOP had never dreamed of winning.

Republican National Committee Chairman Joe Gruters dubbed the September GOP midterm convention in Dallas as "Trumpapalooza."

"Everything that the president has done regarding the economy, regarding the average American worker, I think will lead to votes in November," Gruters told Newsmax later that month.

"Midterm elections are about anger management and failed expectations. They drive the math of turnout," said Paul Shumaker, a Republican strategist in North Carolina, where Democrats flipped the seat held by retiring GOP Sen. Thom Tillis.

"Clearly, Trump failed to meet the economic expectations and also fueled the anger in doing so," he said.

By mid-October, Trump's standing with voters had fallen to levels not seen since Harry S. Truman. In a Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll, the share of U.S. adults who approved of his overall job performance fell to 33 percent, with 66 percent disapproving; 52 percent said they disapproved strongly. Only 28 percent said they approved of his handling of the economy and 27 percent approved of his handling of "the situation with Iran."

An even smaller share, 28 percent, said they approved of Trump's MAGA movement. By more than 2 to 1, Americans said they felt Trump had "gone beyond his authority" as president.

The poll found that registered voters, 58 percent to 39 percent, said they would rather have a Democratic-led Congress acting as a check on Trump than a Republican one to support his agenda. That margin was roughly double what it had been a year earlier.

Unlike notable midterm defeats in 1994 and 2006, when President Bill Clinton and George W. Bush publicly accepted blame for their parties' defeats and committed to changing course in governing, Trump did no such thing.

"I don't like to consider it a defeat for me. I wasn't on the ballot," Trump told Fox News late Tuesday night, a message that was the opposite of what he spent weeks saying on the campaign trail.

"There was a mood in the air, I guess," he continued. "I shouldn't feel guilty because … no matter how good the president is, you lose" in the midterms.

Like Trump, White House advisers blamed the losses entirely on the Republican candidates, insisting that rather than being a rebuke of Trump, the outcome was merely a function of his not being on the ballot. The White House distributed a statement Tuesday night arguing Trump "did a better job promoting many of the candidates on the ballot than the candidates themselves."

"Bloodbath doesn't even begin to describe" voters' reaction to Republicans, said Barrett Marson, an Arizona-based GOP strategist. It was "a complete and total repudiation of one man and his policies," he said, by "an electorate that is upset with being told by President Trump that they are doing better than they are."

"It didn't work for Joe Biden, and Tuesday showed it was the absolute worst strategy Donald Trump could deploy."

The president had failed to explain some of his policies to the public, said Rep. Ralph Norman (R-South Carolina), who lost a primary to Sen. Darline Graham, the Trump-endorsed candidate who lost on Tuesday.

"The Iran war - he needs to explain," Norman said. "When I heard him say, 'The war will end when I say it's going to end,' I'm sorry, that's prideful."

articles.title: Dem AG pulls off upset of sitting Republican governor after blistering campaign in key swing state
articles.summary: Attorney General Aaron Ford ousts Gov. Joe Lombardo to become Nevada's first Black governor, handing Democrats unified control of state government.
articles.body: Nevada Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford has successfully ousted Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo in Nevada, a significant pickup for Democrats in the critical battleground state, The Associated Press projects. Ford's defeat of Lombardo comes in one of the most closely watched gubernatorial races in the country. Ford’s victory makes him Nevada’s first Black governor and gives Democrats control of the governor’s office for the first time since Lombardo defeated Democratic Gov. Steve Sisolak in 2022. Ford, who has served as Nevada’s attorney general since 2019, campaigned on affordability, housing, education, healthcare and protecting access to abortion. He argued that Nevada families were struggling with high housing costs, energy bills and other rising expenses under Lombardo and the Republican administration. FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: THE TOP RACES TO WATCH AS 36 STATES CHOOSE THEIR NEXT GOVERNOR The result could also give Nevada Democrats unified control of state government depending on Tuesday night's election results, with the party already holding majorities in both chambers of the state Legislature. Ford will enter office with a legislative majority aligned with his agenda, although significant disagreements could remain over taxes, education spending, public safety and the state’s business climate. Ford repeatedly criticized Lombardo for aligning himself with President Donald Trump and national Republicans. He argued that Nevada needed a governor who would challenge the administration on federal funding, immigration and voting rights while focusing on the state’s cost-of-living crisis. The Republican incumbent defended his record on public safety, education, economic development and government spending. Lombardo argued that his administration had increased education funding, expanded workforce development and worked to diversify Nevada’s economy beyond tourism and gaming. A BLUE WAVE IN GOVERNORS' MANSIONS COULD HURT FAMILIES MORE THAN A BLUE CONGRESS Lombardo also accused Ford of proposing costly new government programs without explaining how they would be financed. His campaign pointed to a campaign analysis estimating that fully implementing Ford’s platform could cost billions of dollars over four years. Ford rejected that analysis, arguing that Lombardo’s administration had included spending mechanisms and assumptions that were not part of his actual proposals. Ford said his agenda could be accomplished through a combination of existing state resources, federal funding and policy changes. Housing affordability was one of the defining issues of the campaign. Nevada has faced a shortage of affordable homes, particularly in the Las Vegas and Reno areas, while rising rents and mortgage rates have placed pressure on working- and middle-class residents. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The candidates also clashed over energy costs, public education, crime, abortion, immigration and the state’s reliance on tourism and gaming. Nevada’s growing energy demands, including those connected to data centers and other large industrial projects, became another major campaign issue. Lombardo promoted efforts to attract businesses and investment, while Ford argued that economic development should not result in higher costs for residents or additional pressure on the state’s infrastructure. Ford will now face pressure to deliver on his campaign promises while governing a state with significant budget, housing, education and infrastructure challenges. As attorney general, Ford frequently challenged Trump administration policies in court. His election is likely to make Nevada a more prominent Democratic counterweight to the federal government as the state moves toward the 2028 presidential election.

articles.body: El anuncio de la dimisión de Óscar Puente como ministro de Transportes a última hora del lunes ha generado una cadena de reacciones en el mundo de la política, pero también en muchos otros ámbitos. Es el caso de Jordi Évole cuyas reflexiones al respecto de estos asuntos suele dejar un reguero de reacciones. Y lo ha vuelto a hacer toda vez ha conocido la decisión de Puente de dejar su puesto en el Gobierno y no ir en la lista de las elecciones generales del próximo 29 de noviembre. "Se nos había olvidado que la política también podía ser esto", afirmaba el periodista en un mensaje que ya lleva más de más de una decena de miles de 'me gusta' y ha sido compartido más de 3.000 veces. De hecho, este mensaje propio lo ha incorporado junto con el del anuncio de Puente explicando las causas de su decisión: "La decisión sobre mi futuro la tomé los primeros minutos tras la tragedia, cuando tuve conocimiento de ella y así se lo hice saber en primer lugar a mi familia. Un ministro de Transportes de un país como España no puede continuar en su cargo con dos accidentes de esta gravedad en menos de un año, por muy distintos que sean y tenga o no responsabilidad en ellos, pero es una cuestión de dignidad política, coherencia y empatía con las víctimas". Confirmó que renunciaba "a formar parte de las listas electorales del 29 de noviembre". "Formo parte de una organización con casi 150 años de historia. En ella, antes que yo, militó mi madre, que sigue haciéndolo. Y antes que ella, mi abuelo. Por tanto, mi decisión lo único que pretende es estar a la altura, a la altura de mi partido y sobre todo a la altura de los que me precedieron, de los que entregaron todo, y cuando digo todo es todo, por servir a su idea de país y de sociedad, una sociedad más justa e igualitaria".
