articles.title: Democrats win control of House and Senate: Key US midterms takeaways
articles.summary: This is the first time in 20 years that a Republican president has lost both houses of US Congress.
articles.body:
Democrats have won control of Congress after flipping Republican-held House and Senate seats in Texas, South Carolina, Iowa, Michigan and Kansas in the midterm elections.

The results are being seen as a major rebuke to US President Donald Trump’s Republicans, who were previously in control of both houses of Congress.

All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats were contested in Tuesday’s elections, including special elections in Florida and Ohio to fill the seats vacated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President JD Vance.

Voters in 36 states also elected governors, as well as state legislators and local officials.

Counting continued throughout Tuesday evening and night in the US. Results in some races may, however, not be known until Wednesday or later.

These are the key takeaways from this year’s US midterms:

This is the biggest win for the Democrats since the 1990s

Democrats have won 228 seats in the House of Representatives so far, according to the Associated Press’s tally, and are leading in 34 others. That means they could end up with in excess of 260 seats in the House, the party’s biggest strength since 1990, when the Democrats won 267 seats in the lower chamber.

The Republicans held 220 seats in the House after the 2024 elections, while the Democrats had 215.

In the Senate, the upper chamber of Congress, Democrats have won 54 seats and are leading in another, while the Republicans have won 44 seats and are leading in one. To control the Senate, a party needs 51 seats. In the 2024 midterm elections, the Republicans had a majority with 53 seats, while the Democrats won 47 seats.

The Democrats have not had such a clear majority in the Senate since 2008, when the party won 56 seats in the slipstream of Barack Obama’s historic first presidential election.

Amid governors leading in each state, Democrats now have 28 governors, while 20 governors are from the Republican Party. Races in two states currently remain uncalled. Following the 2024 midterms, 27 governors of states were Republican while 23 governors were Democrats.

Not all seats have been called, and Democrats are projected to win more, but they have already flipped 25 seats in the House of Representatives from the Republicans – more than the 21 they took in 2008 when they last held the largest majority in Congress.

This is the first time in 20 years that a Republican president has lost control of both houses of Congress, after George W Bush in 2006.

But Trump’s losses are far deeper than Bush’s: In the 2006 midterms, the Republican strength in the House went down from 232 to 202, while the party’s numbers in the Senate fell from 55 to 49.

This time though, the party is projected to fall short of 180 seats in the House, and is not expected to win more than 45 seats in the Senate.

In the House, in 18 of the 20 midterms held from 1946 to 2022, voters have taken House seats away from the party in power. The average loss was 26 seats across both houses. Only Bill Clinton’s Democrats in 1998 and George W Bush’s Republicans in 2002 bucked that trend by gaining seats or holding them all.

In the Senate, the governing party has lost seats in 13 of the 20 midterms since 1946 but lost overall control of the chamber in only six: 1946, 1954, 1986, 1994, 2006 and 2014.

In the current midterms, while President Trump’s name was not on the ballot, he regularly urged voters to imagine that it was, and the results are seen as a verdict on his presidency.

Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official, has defeated Mike Rogers for senator after a fierce Michigan battle, becoming the first Muslim ever elected to the US Senate.

President Trump has repeatedly targeted El-Sayed, even calling him a “jihadist”.

“He would be the only senator that will have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate,” Trump said during a campaign rally in Michigan.

In his victory speech, El-Sayed said: “America’s greatness is not about ignoring our flaws; it’s the courage that we have to correct them.

“We don’t need to be great again. We need to embrace that thing about us that has always made us great: the will to be more perfect,” he said.

“And right now that means taking on the corporations and the billionaires’ special interests who rigged the system against us,” El-Sayed said.

Democrat Juliana Stratton’s win in the Senate race in Illinois marks the first time in US history that three Black women will be in the Senate at the same time.

Stratton will join Senator Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Senator Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, who were not up for re-election.

Meanwhile, among governors, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms has made history as the first Black woman elected governor in the US.

The former Atlanta mayor emerged victorious over her billionaire opponent, Republican Rick Jackson, who spent more than $200m of his personal fortune in an attempt to succeed popular outgoing Republican Governor Brian Kemp.

Democrat Deb Haaland has made history as the first Native American woman elected governor of a US state, according to The Associated Press news agency’s projections.

Haaland, a former US interior secretary and member of the Laguna Pueblo, defeated Republican Gregg Hull, a former mayor of Rio Rancho, to lead New Mexico.

First Democratic senator to serve in Kansas in 94 years

Democratic US Senate candidate Adam Hamilton has defeated Republican incumbent Roger Marshall in Kansas.

The highly competitive contest between Hamilton, a Methodist pastor, and Marshall stunned political observers given the state’s long history of Republican wins. A Democrat has not won a Senate seat in Kansas since 1932.

“We’re always told to not talk about politics or religion but this is one time we’re trying to save our democracy. The next two years are a pivotal time for our country,” Hamilton had said on Monday.

The race in Kansas was considered consequential to control of the US Senate.

First Democratic senator in Texas in more than 30 years

Democrat James Talarico has defeated Republican Ken Paxton to win the US Senate race in Texas, the first time a Democrat has won state office since 1994.

“The people of Texas were my slingshot,” he told a crowd in Austin in his victory speech. “And tonight, we defeated Goliath.”

Talarico, a member of the Texas House of Representatives, centred his campaign on portraying Paxton as the face of a corrupt political system that allows billionaires to wield outsized political power.

The Democrat’s argument was supercharged after Elon Musk, the world’s richest man and Texas resident, became a key donor in the race.

Talarico also tried to woo moderate Republicans and independents put off by Paxton.

Democrats hold on to California governor

Xavier Becerra, a Democrat who ran on his decades of experience in public office, will take over from California Governor Gavin Newsom as the next governor of the nation’s most populous state.

“If anyone wants to come after California or any one Californian, they better be ready for a fight,” Becerra said on Tuesday night in front of a crowd near Sacramento, according to a report by The Associated Press.

Becerra has become the first Latino elected governor in a state where 40 percent of the population is Hispanic or Latino.

Trump had asked voters to pretend he was on the ballot in the midterm elections.

He also endorsed candidates in South Carolina, North Carolina, Texas, Michigan and others, who were defeated by the Democrats.

In South Carolina, which had not elected a Democratic senator since 1998, Trump backed Darline Graham. But Democrat Annie Andrews won the seat.

In North Carolina, Trump had endorsed former national Republican campaign official Michael Whatley, who was beaten by Democratic Governor Roy Cooper.

In Texas, Trump promoted Attorney General Ken Paxton. But Democrat Talarico won the race.

Then in Michigan, Former US Representative Mike Rogers, Trump’s choice in Michigan, was defeated by Democrat El-Sayed.

Speaking to Fox News, Trump said: “I think the Democrats did a good job. I really do. I think they did a good job. They fought hard.”

He added that there was a “mood in the air” and said, “I shouldn’t feel guilty.”

Opinion polls ahead of the midterms had pointed to Democrats having a good night and winning the House and possibly the Senate.

But some pre-election polls were also cautious in calling it a complete win for Democrats since polls in the recent past have been off the mark.

Polling in the US began with newspapers collecting local opinions in the 1880s. Predictions have often been right, historically.

But in more recent years, they have often been horribly wrong.

In 2016, opinion polls correctly predicted the popular vote for Hillary Clinton, but also had her winning the presidency, comfortably, in states like Pennsylvania, Michigan and Wisconsin, which Trump ultimately won. Their forecast of Clinton winning the Electoral College was also proved wrong.

Polls were off in 2020 again, when COVID-19 restrictions greatly limited surveys. Most polls correctly predicted that Joe Biden would win the Electoral College and national votes. But they significantly overestimated support for Democrats by an “unusual magnitude”, according to the American Association for Public Opinion Research (AAPOR), while undercounting voters backing Trump.

Then, in 2022, polls got it wrong the other way – for the midterm elections. Some polls suggested that Republicans would sweep the House and Senate that year. In the end, the race was much closer, at least in the Senate, where neither party won a majority. Democrats ended up gaining narrow control with 51- 49, with the support of independents who caucus with them. Republicans, as predicted, won the House 222 – 213.

Then, in the 2024 presidential election, public opinion polls had predicted a neck-and-neck race between Donald Trump and Vice President Kamala Harris . Yet eventually, Trump cruised to a comfortable victory, defying most polls.

But this year, opinion polls have been in track with voter’s opinions, with many saying they voted for change.

Gary Colbert, who cast his ballot on the west side of Detroit, lamented the rise in fuel prices due to the US-Israel war on Iran, and added that Trump and “his cronies” are negatively affecting people’s lives, “and they don’t care”.

His wife, Shirley Colbert, said “some changes need to be made” to address the cost-of-living crisis.

“I’m going with the Democrat; I’m not going to go with Republicans because we have one of those in office right now, and we see what’s going on not just in Michigan but across the United States,” she told Al Jazeera.

Texas voter Monique Orellana, 46, had a message for every candidate regardless of party: “Do your job!”

“I would vote for Republicans if I felt they were going to do what they said they were going to do. Right now I’m not feeling it,” she told Al Jazeera.

“It’s name-calling and stuff like that. They don’t ever give anything about their policies. It’s just like ‘Talafreako’ [a nickname for Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico coined by his Republican opponent, Ken Paxton, and adopted by US President Donald Trump] and all of that,” she said

“Trump said he wasn’t going to start a war, and he did anyway. And he said he was going to fix the price of groceries on day one. They went up anyway. I still don’t know why they started this war and why it’s still going. But right now it’s just hope,” she added.

articles.title: Republicans start to point fingers at Trump after severe midterms loss
articles.summary: Trump's political lieutenants are trying to shift the blame onto lazy candidates, but Republicans on Capitol Hill and beyond are not buying it.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump's allies on Wednesday tiptoed their way toward once unthinkable territory: blaming the president.

The unusual candor followed sweeping GOP defeats across the country, a repudiation of the president that matched some of the party's worst fears. Some pointed to the Iran war and its effect on gas and grocery prices. Others pointed to the president's demeanor.

"There's a little bit of a reckoning in the Republican Party about where they go," said Matt Dole, chair of the GOP in deep red Licking County, Ohio. "I think you're going to see a part of the Republican Party advocate for a return to normalcy, which is not repudiating Trump's ideology and policies, but will repudiate Trump's style."

"It sounds a little ironic," failed Maine Republican Gov. candidate Bobby Charles told POLITICO. "but I am nevertheless optimistic for the future because Trump's going to be gone in two years."

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Trump and his advisors, meanwhile, blamed a myriad of factors, including Fox News, RINOs and "lazy" candidates — even as the party resoundingly lost both chambers of government and the blue wave rolled through deep red Texas, South Carolina, Iowa and Kansas.

Trump singled out Texas GOP governor Greg Abbott, who he called a "RINO," and absolved himself of blame, claiming Republicans would have won "in a landslide" had he been on the ballot.

Abbott did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Trump's adviser Alex Bruesewitz blamed the GOP's poor performance on candidates he described as "uninspiring, lazy and thoroughly ineffective communicators" — explicitly calling out Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.), who struggled throughout the course of his campaign to gain traction against Democratic incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff.

The Collins campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

One GOP operative working on multiple midterm races said it was a "lazy excuse" to blame candidate quality. "This is more than just one lazy candidate here. I mean, the chair of the … NRCC is losing his election."

Still, other Republicans turned their ire on the GOP-controlled Congress.

"The Republican Party needs to have a conversation with itself about how to listen to the voters and present meaningful policy reform that impacts their lives," said Gina Swoboda, the former chair of Arizona's Republican Party and a longtime Trump ally. "This Congress did not do a single thing that I can name that meaningfully impacted the working class and middle class."

Bruesewitz expressed dismay that some of those candidates boarded Air Force One and left their states five days before Election Day, after Trump had traveled to campaign for them.

"They're so dependent and so reliant on the president," Bruesewitz said. "The president's strength has allowed Republicans to coast for a decade. His endorsement has cleared the field for them in their primaries and oftentimes in general elections. Most of them have never had to fight in a tough race, so they forgot the basics of campaigning and communicating in a digital era." Top Trump officials had already hinted at that plan in interviews with POLITICO in the lead up to the election.

Republicans on Capitol Hill and beyond, who have been preparing for the bloodbath and recriminations, were not buying it. They argued that flat characterization of Republican candidates as lazy could not possibly be applied to every vulnerable Republican who lost — and that Trump and the aides around him ought to look in the mirror.

But tellingly, they refused to put their name behind it.

"We are beyond candidate quality. It's a bloodbath," one senior Senate GOP official said. "Trump did this."

A Republican operative working on swing state campaigns said Tuesday was a perfect storm "of just incompetence."

"The people in the White House didn't do anything to stop him from engaging on things that were actively making everything worse because he was ignoring what the voters were caring about," the operative said.

Iowa Republicans are facing tight races in the House and Senate as they aim to keep Republican control over the battleground state. (Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

articles.title: Bonta says he'll counter DOJ election monitors with observers of his own
articles.summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta is deploying state election observers amid concerns the DOJ's federal monitoring could intimidate voters.
articles.body: California Attorney General Rob Bonta said Tuesday afternoon that his office will deploy election observers in response to concerns that Justice Department monitors could intimidate voters. Bonta said California was taking the same approach it used during the previous two elections, when the state dispatched its own observers alongside federal monitors. The DOJ's Civil Rights Division has sent 1,000 monitors across the country to ensure election integrity and protect Americans' right to vote, a plan that has been public knowledge for months. The monitors will be personnel from across the DOJ, U.S. Attorney's Offices and employees from the Office of Personnel Management. The department confirmed Tuesday that while federal election monitoring is routine, this year's operation is the largest in its history, with monitors deployed to all 50 states for the first time. DOJ FIRES BACK AT DEM AG OVER ELECTION DAY GUIDANCE TELLING OFFICIALS WHEN TO CALL COPS ON FEDERAL AGENTS The DOJ also released a list of cities where monitors are being deployed. In California, they are being sent to Los Angeles, Alameda, Sacramento and San Diego. Bonta and other critics have argued that the unusually large federal presence could spook voters or discourage some from casting ballots. Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who leads the Civil Rights Division, told Bloomberg in an August interview that the role of DOJ election monitors would be to observe election practices and pursue investigations into any possible instances of fraud after the fact — not to intervene directly while people are voting. In Tuesday's announcement, the DOJ added that monitors will also be responsible for ensuring that polling places are accessible for those with disabilities. DOJ OFFICIAL DEFENDS TRUMP'S NONCITIZEN VOTER PROBE ON '60 MINUTES,' ACCUSES SHOW OF EDITING OUT HER ANSWERS In her Bloomberg interview, Dhillon said the election monitors would respect the laws of whichever states they end up in. Many states restrict monitors from entering polling places and require them to remain behind designated boundaries outside. "We respect state law," Dhillon told Bloomberg at the time. "We reach out to the states. If their perimeter is 150 yards, we respect that." Dhillon also pointed out that the DOJ sent more than 80 monitors to observe primary elections across seven states this year, including locations in Minnesota, Michigan, Florida, Wyoming, South Carolina, Massachusetts and New Hampshire. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The nationwide deployment appeared to be proceeding without major incident Tuesday afternoon, with no significant confrontations involving federal monitors publicly reported. This comes after the Supreme Court on Monday rejected the Trump administration's effort to require California election officials to segregate ballots cast by 20,000 voters the DOJ believes are noncitizens.

articles.title: How Trump and Republicans lost the 2026 midterm elections, according to The AP Voter Poll
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — After more than a decade with Donald Trump at the epicenter of U. politics, most voters appear exhausted and exasperated by him, according...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — After more than a decade with Donald Trump at the epicenter of U.S. politics, most voters appear exhausted and exasperated by him, according to The AP Voter Poll , a survey of midterm voters in all 50 states.

The president's failure to deliver on key promises — most prominently, his vows to tame inflation, which has worsened instead — clearly weighed on his fellow Republicans in Tuesday's midterm elections for the House and the Senate . The polling shows that voters generally saw Trump as being more focused on his own fortune and gold-leafed existence than their needs.

The president also helped elevate candidates with obvious flaws, amplifying their struggles in an already challenging year. He suggested in a Tuesday evening interview with Fox News Channel that Democrats "fought hard" and that the Republican base "didn't like the candidates" he had endorsed because some of his picks were not fully loyal to him.

But the poll also contains a serious note of caution for Democrats. Many voters dislike the party — and while Democrats hold an advantage on key issues such as the economy, their edge is relatively slim. About 7 in 10 voters said Congress is not doing enough to provide checks and balances for the president, setting the bar for Democrats who won back the Senate and the House.

It was impossible for GOP candidates to hide from inflation . Voters could see it clearly in their receipts from grocery stores and gasoline stations . The financial blow of an auto repair or a utility bill after a sweltering summer was inescapable. And even in Republican strongholds such as Texas, the drag caused by inflation helped Democrats.

About 2 in 10 Texas voters said inflation had imposed "severe" hardship on them and their family — and about three-quarters of this group backed Democrat James Talarico for the Senate. An additional 6 in 10 voters, roughly, said inflation had led to "moderate" hardship, and Talarico won the majority of these voters, too.

That same pattern repeated in state after state. Nationally, voters who said they were "very concerned" about everyday costs — including groceries, healthcare and gas — overwhelmingly said they voted for the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race.

But it wasn't just the inflation itself that mattered. Voters nationwide pinned the blame on Trump for his tariffs , his war in Iran and his unfulfilled campaign promise two years ago to bring down prices.

Asked about the impact of Trump's policies, about two-thirds of voters nationwide said they had made the economy worse. And out of this group, about 8 in 10 said they backed the Democratic candidate.

More than half of voters nationally said government corruption was "crucial" for their vote for Congress. That was a little higher than the share who said the cost of living was "crucial," a striking finding in a year when about 6 in 10 voters said they were personally "very concerned" about the cost of food and groceries.

Meanwhile, despite Republicans' suggestion that voters cared little about Trump making more than $1 billion last year from meme coins and cryptocurrency, most voters saw Trump as obsessed with his own interests. During his second term, Trump solicited donations from powerful companies to build his desired White House ballroom after having surprised the country by rapidly demolishing what had been the building's East Wing .

That tenor set at the top spilled over into business deals for his family and other deals by his associates involving pardons and federal policies.

Ultimately, about two-thirds of voters said Trump does not have the right priorities — and the overwhelming majority of these voters supported Democratic House candidates.

For much of the past two years, Trump acted on his own .

Much of the Republican-controlled House and Senate barely objected to his whims. He laid off federal workers , imposed sweeping new tariffs, launched the war with Iran, remodeled Washington in gold paint, threatened the Federal Reserve , the Kennedy Center and the Smithsonian Institution and bullied a bevy of longtime allies.

Voters made it clear that they want more congressional oversight.

About 7 in 10 voters said Congress was not doing enough to provide checks and balances for the presidency, including about 4 in 10 Republicans.

Swing voters don't really love Democrats, even if they voted for them

Despite Democrats' victories, voters did not deliver a ringing endorsement of the party as a whole. Many voters expressed frustration with both parties: On the economy, foreign policy, healthcare, taxes and immigration, roughly 2 in 10 voters said "neither" party was better equipped to handle these issues. An even larger share of voters said neither party would be better at addressing government corruption or artificial intelligence.

Those skeptical voters generally broke for Democrats.

But it wasn't because the party was overwhelmingly popular. Only about half of voters had a "somewhat" or "strongly" favorable view of the Democratic Party. That was higher than the approximately 4 in 10 who viewed the GOP positively, but not by much. About 2 in 10 voters who supported Democratic candidates had a negative view of the party as a whole.

Instead, in key races, voters seemed to be looking to Democratic candidates for change. In Maine, for instance, most voters who said having a candidate with "the right experience" mattered most to their Senate decision chose Republican incumbent Susan Collins. But more voters cared about bringing about "needed change," and they favored Democrat Troy Jackson .

Trump endorsed Republicans who turned off voters — and that put areas that were once safely with the GOP at risk.

After Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina died in July, the president chose the late senator's sister, Darline Graham, to fill his seat. The new Sen. Graham then promptly decided to seek election and struggled on foreign policy questions that were once her brother's forte.

About 6 in 10 voters in the South Carolina Senate race said she lacked the experience to serve in the Senate.

During the Texas Republican primary, Trump ultimately backed the state's attorney general, Ken Paxton , over its sitting senator, John Cornyn. Paxton was scandal-ridden and had been impeached but not convicted. About two-thirds of Texas Senate voters said he lacked the character to be a senator.

The president prized loyalty in Republican candidates. That hurt Republican candidates in many states.

In North Carolina, as in several other states, about 6 in 10 voters said the state's Republican Senate nominee, Michael Whatley, was "too supportive" of Trump. They chose former Gov. Roy Cooper , a Democrat, for the Senate instead.

Follow the AP's coverage of the 2026 elections at .

The AP Voter Poll is a survey of the American electorate conducted by SSRS for The Associated Press, ABC News, CBS News, CNN, FOX News Media, NBC News and Versant. The survey blends probability-based and non-probability-based interviews with registered voters in all 50 states conducted from Oct. 19 to Nov. 3 in Alaska and Oct. 22 to Nov. 3 in all other states. A detailed methodology statement is available. The margin of sampling error is plus or minus 0.6 percentage points for the full sample.

articles.title: How Trump ignited a midterm drubbing for Republicans
articles.summary: Americans delivered an emphatic repudiation of President Trump Tuesday as Democrats took control of both chambers of Congress by wide margins.
articles.body:
WASHINGTON — Americans delivered an emphatic repudiation of President Donald Trump's second term Tuesday as Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress by wide margins and scored wins deep in red territory after running against Trump's unpopular war in Iran and his economic agenda.

In a midterm election that Trump embraced as a referendum on himself — actively pleading to his supporters to "pretend I'm on the ballot" — Republicans were dealt a crippling blow as a massive blue tsunami swept away battleground GOP candidates.

"It seems like voters took Trump seriously when he told them to vote as if he were on the ballot," said Sarah Matthews, who served as a deputy press secretary during Trump's first administration, adding that the president "has no one to blame but himself."

Republicans lost Senate races in Texas , South Carolina, Kansas, Ohio and Iowa ‒ GOP bastions that Trump carried by double digits in 2024 and to which he personally made multiple visits in the homestretch of the midterm campaign .

Texas hadn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988; and Kansas not since 1932, when Hebert Hoover was president . Democrats were projected to win nearly every key battleground Senate race despite largely fighting on political terrain that strongly favored Republicans, while also flipping enough Republican-held seats to comfortably win the House.

"In sweeping and decisive victories, the American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption, and incompetence of the failed lame duck president, Donald J. Trump," Democratic Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff said in his victory speech.

The staggering GOP loses amounted to a resounding midterm thumping for Republicans on Trump's watch — one that the president quickly tried to distance himself from.

"I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!" Trump wrote on social media as it became clear the GOP was heading for a dismal election night.

The outcome makes Trump a lame-duck president legislatively for his final two years in office, threatening the iron grip he's held on the Republican Party for the past decade — particularly as attention shifts to a 2028 presidential election that won't feature him as the party's nominee.

Historically, sitting presidents with Trump's level of unpopularity stay far away from the campaign trail during midterms to allow their party's candidates to distance themselves from the White House.

But Trump, despite his record-low approval ratings hovering below 35%, barnstormed the country with more than two dozen rallies in a push to energize MAGA supporters — even if his presence might have undercut the same Republican Senate candidates he aimed to help.

In an election dominated by Americans' concerns about the economy and rising cost of living, Trump mocked the term "affordability" as a creation of Democrats and said higher gas prices were a "small price to pay" for achieving his administration's aims in Iran.

Rather than focusing on the economy during his final speech before Election Day, Trump devoted the bulk of his closing argument to talking about his recent renovations to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. Trump boasted about clearing algae from the D.C. landmark and installing the best granite, waiting until more than 20 minutes into his speech to finally mention an election was taking place the following day.

Trump delivers closing midterm message at Reflecting Pool

Longtime pollster Frank Luntz said voters who went from casting ballots for Trump in past elections to backing Democrats felt misled by his campaign promise to lower costs. Luntz pointed to a focus group he conducted of Republican midterm voters from Texas, Ohio, Georgia and South Carolina who supported Trump in 2024 but voted for Democrats in Senate races this year.

"They felt disappointed and just disillusioned with what's happened over the past two years, specifically over affordability," Luntz said. "They all ‒ no matter what part of the country they were from ‒ complained about how high prices had gotten and how they had been promised lower prices."

"This is no endorsement of the Democratic Party or the Democratic agenda," Luntz added. "It was rejection on what happened, or more importantly what didn't happen, over the last two years."

The Reflecting Pool event encapsulated a broader theme that handcuffed Republicans: Throughout the campaign, Trump seemed more interested in talking about his legacy Washington projects — his White House ballroom and helipad, his plans for a triumphal arch and renovated Washington golf course — than kitchen-table issues that registered with voters.

Democrats capitalized on the disconnect.

A senior White House official, who spoke to USA TODAY on the condition of anonymity, defended Trump's midterm strategy, arguing he put the party in a better position with a relentless campaign schedule that included 30 events in 20 states over a four-week stretch.

Trump would've been criticized if he hadn't been aggressive in trying to help the party, the official said.

After the Democratic rout was on, Trump conceded the war in Iran weighed on Republican candidates, telling Fox News in an interview, "I think a part of it was Iran."

Yet he was still apparently unwilling to accept blame for the devasting outcome for Republicans.

"I don't like to consider it a defeat for me. I wasn't on the ballot, if you're on the ballot it's different than if you're not on the ballot," Trump told Fox News.

The president's decision to thrust himself into the center of the midterm campaign despite voters' deep misgivings about his performance may have helped sink candidates in key races by tying them more closely to him. Some tried to distance themselves from Trump, but were swept out anyway.

Some of the most stinging GOP loses came in states where Trump endorsed close allies in the primary who went on to struggle in the general election. Perhaps the most glaring example was the scandal-plagued Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who unseated four-term Sen. John Cornyn in the state's Senate primary with the president's backing but consistently trailed Democrat James Talarico in polls before his defeat on Nov. 3. Trump's endorsement of Darline Graham, a political novice and the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, boosted her through the primary, but resulted in a shocking general election defeat in a state Trump carried by 18 percentage points.

"It certainly didn't help that he handpicked weak candidates who only made matters worse," Matthews said.

Ultimately, though, even Republicans viewed as strong candidates were unable to overcome the dismal political climate for the GOP, one driven by deep discontent with Trump. That includes Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, a political survivor who had overcome poor polling in previous elections and carved out a reputation as an independent-minded moderate willing to vote against Trump. She lost her bid for a sixth term to Democrat Troy Jackson.

"Bad night is an understatement," said Charlie Black, a Republican strategist. "We lost every seat in play and some that we did not know were in play."

The results leave the president politically weakened, facing a hostile Democratic Congress that is eager to rein him in.

Democrats have signaled they will launch an aggressive oversight campaign, with Trump administration officials facing a barrage of congressional hearings and potential subpoenas.

Trump's critics are eager to shut down his controversial second term agenda, which has featured mass deportations, sweeping tariffs and military actions that have drawn strong criticism.

The president told Fox News on election night that he hopes to work with Democrats, mentioning immigration as an area where both sides might be able to come together.

"I could work with them on many, many things," Trump said.

Yet he also vowed to wield his veto pen liberally to block Democrat priorities and force them to negotiate, saying: "After a couple months of vetoes, they'll call and they'll say 'How do we get this stuff done?' And we'll work together."

Trump, however, also faces the possibility of growing dissent within the ranks of his own party, with the midterms showing the perils of Republicans aligning too closely with the president.

The election could be an inflection point for the GOP, which Trump has dominated for a decade but now must grapple with his waning appeal to voters and find a path back to winning battleground states ahead of the 2028 election.

"When the very person you've spent years defending starts costing you elections, that loyalty becomes a whole lot harder to justify," Matthews said.
authors: Joey Garrison and Zac Anderson, USA TODAY

articles.title: Mississippi Senate race too close to call
articles.summary: Mississippi’s Senate race remained too close to call early Wednesday, with Democratic challenger Scott Colom holding a razor-thin lead over Sen. Cindy Hyde-S...
articles.body:
Mississippi's Senate race remained too close to call early Wednesday, with Democratic challenger Scott Colom holding a razor-thin lead over Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R) of less than 1 percentage point.

With nearly all ballots counted, Colom led Hyde-Smith by a little more than 2,000 votes — 461,370 to 459,201 — as of early Wednesday morning, according to Decision Desk HQ .

The contest has put the reliably red state in the national spotlight as Democrats celebrate massive victories in Tuesday's midterm elections, winning control of both chambers of Congress and flipping several Republican-held Senate seats.

A victory for Colom, a district attorney in the Magnolia State, would mark the eighth Senate seat Democrats have flipped this election cycle and a stunning political shift in Mississippi, which President Trump won by more than 20 percentage points in 2024.

The race drew increasing attention in the closing days of the campaign as Democrats saw an opportunity to unseat Hyde-Smith, who was widely viewed as weak on the campaign trail, despite the state's strong GOP lean.

Colom's showing in the contest comes amid a wave of blue victories in states considered to be Republican strongholds, including Kansas , where Adam Hamilton defeated Sen. Roger Marshall (R), and South Carolina , where Annie Andrews ousted Sen. Darline Graham (R).

In Texas, Democrat James Talarico defeated Trump-backed state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R), delivering the party its first Senate victory in the Lone Star State in nearly four decades.

Mississippi has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982, when former Sen. John Stennis won his final term.

articles.title: Five reasons why Republicans lost so badly
articles.summary: From angry voters to an unpopular president, here is why Americans in traditional Republican areas turned to Democrats.
articles.body:
The Democrats have swept to victory in the US midterm elections, taking control of Congress.

While the incumbent president's party generally tends to have a bad night in these elections, the scale of the Republican defeat is being viewed as a resounding rejection of Donald Trump's two years in the White House.

From angry voters to an unpopular president , here are five reasons why the Republicans lost so many seats .

From coast to coast, voters across the US have been grappling with the soaring cost of essentials. That anger was palpable on the ground in key races.

"Gas prices, grocery prices, everything's going up," one North Carolina voter told the BBC ahead of the elections, adding that she had switched her vote from Republican to Democratic this election.

Prices increased by 3.7% in the year to September, driven higher by fuel and energy prices. Average US retail diesel prices in early October were just shy of the record of $6.52 (£4.83) per gallon seen in September, according to government data.

Almost eight in 10 voters (79%) said inflation had caused them and their family a severe or moderate hardship in the past year, according to data from voter polls.

And more than six in 10 respondents laid the blame for that at the feet of Trump, saying they thought higher than usual prices were because of the president's policies.

A major factor in surging prices has been the war with Iran which the US and Israel launched in February.

Fuel prices then shot up after Tehran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation, strangling a key artery for the passage of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG).

US voters have been paying the price at the petrol pump ever since.

The war has proved broadly unpopular with most Americans. For Maga Republicans it also felt like a broken promise in Trump's America First campaign agenda in which he pledged there would be no more wars .

Around six in 10 (63%) of those asked in a voter poll said the US made the wrong decision to take military action against Iran.

Separately, three-quarters of voters (74%) said the conflict was a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress.

The morning after the election, Trump conceded the war had played a role in the defeat but insisted in an interview on Fox that he had no choice but to intervene to stop Iran getting a nuclear weapon.

The scale and breadth of this Democratic wave was made possible by some strong candidates who came across as authentic, especially in traditional Republican heartlands.

They stuck to a disciplined message about the cost of living and healthcare access.

Former teacher James Talarico and pastor Adam Hamilton also talked about their faith in a way that struck a chord in Texas and Kansas respectively.

In South Carolina, Democrat Annie Andrews pulled off a shock upset. A former paediatrician, her focus on health care affordability resonated in a country where many see the system as broken.

Former public health official Abdul El-Sayed, who triumphed in Michigan to keep that seat Democratic, made getting "money out of politics, money in your pocket" a key slogan.

Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, who won re-election in Georgia, made the cost of living and corruption a central message. The 39-year-old's comfortable victory in a state Trump won twice will only fuel rumours of a 2028 presidential run.

Even Trump himself praised the Democrats, telling Fox News they "did a good job".

Conversely, some Republican candidates like Ken Paxton in Texas were criticised for running poor campaigns that were not focused enough on voters' concerns.

4. Trump's unpopularity a drag on Republicans

Two of the issues voters were most unhappy with - rocketing prices and the Iran War - were directly linked to the president.

His approval ratings had even fallen among Republican voters, which made some of these states which backed him in 2024 especially vulnerable.

He urged voters to imagine he was on the ballot in an effort to galvanise his supporters.

But after more than a decade as the central figure in American politics, some see these results as evidence that the glitz may be wearing off Trump's brand.

Against a backdrop of increasing anger, making himself the focus of the Republican campaign was risky and appears to have backfired .

In the months leading up to the vote, polling indicated that many Americans wanted Trump to focus more on their concerns about rocketing prices.

In his final campaign speech on Monday in Washington DC, he talked at length about his controversial renovation project of the Reflecting Pool behind him.

Listen to Americast: Democrats make historic shift in US politics

5. Hispanic and black voters shift again

Two years ago a move towards Republicans among some Hispanic and black voters helped Trump secure a decisive win. That seems to have reversed in these midterms.

Democrats claimed all three House races in the overwhelmingly Hispanic congressional districts along the Texas-Mexico border.

Majority-Hispanic counties moved more than 22 percentage points against Republican Senate candidates, compared with the 2024 presidential election, according to a New York Times analysis.

The change is more than any other major demographic group in the country, data reporter Jeff Adelson said.

The shift comes amid widespread anger at immigration enforcement, with a majority (56%) of Americans saying they have an unfavourable opinion of ICE, according to the Pew Research Center.

Counties with a black majority also moved significantly towards Democratic candidates in Senate races.

The Senate race is on a knife-edge in Mississippi, which has the largest share of black voters of any US state with around 37%.

If Scott Colom can win, he would become the first Democrat elected to the Senate in Mississippi since 1982.

articles.summary: (The Center Square) – Amid a devastating loss for Republicans Tuesday night into Wednesday morning, President Donald Trump has remained defiant as he takes s...
articles.body:
(The Center Square) – Amid a devastating loss for Republicans Tuesday night into Wednesday morning, President Donald Trump has remained defiant as he takes stock of his party's showing.

Trump, who stayed at the White House Tuesday, hosted a watch party in the East Room, flanked by members of his cabinet and administration.

Once it became clear Republicans would lose control of both chambers of Congress, the president claimed the loss was because he wasn't on the ballot.

"I wasn't on the ballot and if I was, we would have won in a landslide!" Trump posted Tuesday night.

Despite the loss, Trump commended Democrats, telling Fox News that "Democrats did a good job," adding that "they fought hard."

The president added that he is willing to work with Democrats, including on the hot-button issue of immigration; however, he warned that he will be using his power to veto bills.

"After a couple of months of vetoes, they'll call, and they'll say, 'How do we get this stuff done?' And we'll work together," he said. "I have the power of veto."

Trump acknowledged that the massive loss was in part due to Trump's decision to strike Iran and the subsequent high energy prices.

The president added that he thought Republican candidates would have done better; he even took aim at Texas Republican Gov. Gregg Abbott, accusing him of turning into a RINO (Republican in name only) recently.

Congress is scheduled to reconvene next week, with several confirmations remaining on the line and a looming government funding deadline.

The president has no open press events on his schedule for Wednesday as of the time of publication.

Trump's last public event was held Monday afternoon in front of the Reflecting Pool as he used the refurbishing of a historic landmark as an opportunity to make a last-ditch effort to make a case for Republicans ahead of the midterms.

The president used the last month of the election to host more than 30 rallies in battleground states.

articles.title: JASON CHAFFETZ: Five timeless political lessons that got lost in 2026
articles.summary: Republicans face hard midterm election lessons on candidate quality, primary elections and endorsements as House and Senate leadership changes loom.
articles.body: While the leadership of the House and Senate is changing, the fundamentals of American politics have not. In all the finger pointing that will ensue over the coming weeks, some things should already be clear. Regardless of where the last ballots fall, the basic principles of American politics remain the same. Voters still respond to the same things they always have. As Republicans look to 2028, they must double down on the basics of campaigning that stand the test of time. 1. Candidate quality matters. Fielding the better candidate is not optional. It may not always be definitive, but it is foundational. A candidate who cannot connect with people, articulate a positive vision of the future or run a disciplined campaign operation will eventually be vulnerable. Celebrity, political dynasties, comfortable incumbents or last-minute appointments do not automatically translate into votes. LIZ PEEK: THERE MAY BE A SILVER LINING IN TRUMP'S BRUTAL MIDTERM DEFEAT 2. Results must be felt. A majority is judged by outcomes people can feel, not by legislative talking points. The Senate had two years. Voters do not grade on process. They grade on whether prices at the pump and the grocery store stopped rising, whether their communities felt safe and whether the problems they voted to fix in 2024 actually got fixed. A Senate that refuses to build on the work of the House, maximize judicial appointments or secure the president’s signature election security promise is asking for a loss. Excuses do not win midterms. Outcomes do. A majority that is perpetually in recess and does not deliver consistent results should expect to pay dearly. That is neither new nor complicated. 3. Volume is not a strategy. Too much money is spent on strategies with too little value, often in ways that simply annoy voters. Exaggerated attack ads that no one believes, incessant text messages that interrupt dinner and uninvited fundraising solicitations that clog up inboxes do not persuade people. They irritate them. Voters have learned to tune out the noise and campaigns that treat volume as a strategy end up wasting money while making the people they need less likely to listen. Consultants who still measure success by how many times they can hit the same voter are not helping their candidates. They are training people to ignore them. 4. Candidate choice is a local decision. Primaries exist for a reason. Putting a finger on the scale for a candidate the voters have not fully affirmed is a recipe for disaster. Democrats learned that the hard way when they elevated Kamala Harris without a real primary contest. Republicans got a reminder this cycle in South Carolina, where Darline Graham was appointed to her late brother’s seat and then heavily backed through the primary process. She won the nomination, but voters in a deep-red state ultimately rejected the candidate who had been chosen for them. Skipping or short-circuiting the primary process does not protect the seat. It risks it. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION 5. Endorsements do not win or lose races. They matter when you are nobody trying to become somebody. For federal office, most voters do not care about the long list of endorsements. They look at the candidate standing in front of them and the message that candidate is offering. National figures, party committees and celebrity names generate headlines and fundraising, but they rarely move the final margin the way candidates and consultants claim. Campaigns waste too much time chasing them. Voters make their own decisions and do so primarily on authenticity and plans for the future. The question is whether the people running campaigns will treat them as optional again or whether they will finally stop looking for shortcuts that keep failing.

articles.title: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan U.S. Senate race, makes history
articles.summary: (The Center Square) – Progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has won Michigan’s U. S.
articles.body:
(The Center Square) – Progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has won Michigan's U.S. Senate race, with Democrats ending with in control of both chambers of Congress after Tuesday's midterm elections.

"It is my honor and privilege to be headed to the US Senate to serve the great state of Michigan," El-Sayed said early Wednesday morning. "Michigan, we did what they said couldn't be done. We won. Together. Now the real work begins."

El-Sayed is the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate – defeating Republican Mike Rogers. He will succeed Democratic U.S. Sen. Gary Peters, who was first elected in 2014. Peters announced in January 2025 that he would not seek reelection.

With more than 95% of the vote in, El-Sayed leads with 52.5% of the vote to Rogers' 45.5%. Nearly 5 million Michiganders cast ballots, marking the highest turnout of any midterm election in state history.

In 2024, Michigan's U.S. Senate race was decided by less than half a percentage point, with Democrat Elissa Slotkin narrowly defeating Rogers. Rogers returned as the Republican nominee in 2026 after securing the party's nomination unopposed.

Rogers has not yet released a statement conceding the race.

The race was the most expensive in Michigan history, with more than $250 million in disclosed spending alone.

articles.title: Trump: Iran war partially to blame for GOP midterm losses
articles.summary: President Trump partially blamed the ongoing war with Iran for the GOP’s sweeping midterm losses in the midterms — but said he would have done it again. Trum...
articles.body:
President Trump partially blamed the ongoing war with Iran for the GOP's sweeping midterm losses in the midterms — but said he would have done it again.

Trump told The Wall Street Journal that the Middle East conflict, now in its eighth month, "was a piece of it" in an election night interview .

Gas and diesel prices have skyrocketed in the U.S. and globally since the war started in late February, increasing voter frustrations after the president campaigned on ending foreign wars in 2024. Trump told the Journal that he thought high fuel costs were the biggest factor behind his party's losses Tuesday.

Republicans suffered a historically large defeat in Tuesday's midterms, losing at least seven Senate seats, Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) projected. Two races, Mississippi and Alaska, remain uncalled as of Wednesday morning.

The GOP also lost 30 seats in the House, with more than 20 races left to be projected, according to DDHQ.

Some of the Republican candidates who faltered were ones handpicked or endorsed by Trump himself. These candidates include Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R), who lost to Democrat James Talarico by 12 points, and South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham (R), who lost in an upset to Democrat Annie Andrews by 4 points.

The president backed Paxton in his primary challenge against Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and supported Graham in a special primary after urging South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster (R) to tap her to fill the seat left open by her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R).

He told the Journal that he could "only do so much" to help Republican candidates, admitting some had "flaws."

"I tried to help them," Trump said of Graham and Paxton. "Darline worked very hard, they worked hard. But they both didn't make it."

At the start of next year, the administration will be met with a more hostile Congress than what he has faced during the first two years of his term.

Trump told the Journal that he was willing to work with Democrats — similar to his sentiment after the 2018 midterms — but pointed out he retains the ability to veto any bills passed through Congress in the final two years of his presidency.

"I think we'll work with the Democrats, and we'll get along very well with them," he said. "If we don't, we'll be very tough on them, they'll be very tough on us."

The president also told the Journal and The New York Times that he would accept the results of the election, after warning of widespread fraud and cheating by his opponents in years past.

articles.title: Republicans blame Trump for midterm losses, while Trump points elsewhere
articles.summary: Donald Trump has turned the blame toward candidates he previously endorsed, like Texas Gov. Greg Abbott.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — A blue wave has swept the country, turning deep-red states like Texas blue. In response, Republicans have taken to blaming President Donald Trump for the losses; meanwhile, Trump is pointing the blame elsewhere.

GOP midterm defeat 'reflection of Trump's agenda': Official

"I think much of what we are seeing tonight is a reflection of Trump's agenda, particularly our continued involvement in Iran, high gas prices, inflation and the lack of focus on issues affecting everyday Americans," a statewide Republican official told Scripps News.

"It sounds a little ironic, but I am nonetheless optimistic for the future because Trump's going to be gone in two years," Republican candidate Bobby Charles told POLITICO.

Charles lost to Democrat Hannah Pingree in Maine's governor's race.

Trump: War with Iran partially to blame for GOP losses

Trump, in an interview with the Wall Street Journal, acknowledged the war with Iran was partially to blame for Republicans losing both the House and Senate.

"Iran was a piece of it," Trump told the WSJ but defended his decision to go to war, saying he does not regret it. "I don't think about it. I did the right thing. I would have done it again."

In an interview with CNN prior to the midterms, former GOP Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene said a Republican loss would be a referendum on Donald Trump's betrayal.

"I think it's a complete referendum on Donald Trump — his betrayal, where he promised no more foreign wars and to bring world peace, not releasing the Epstein files," Taylor Greene said. "And also, not listening to everyday Americans who are saying, 'We cannot afford the cost of living, we cannot afford health insurance, we cannot afford these high prices of gas and diesel.' While he is constantly bragging about a ballroom and his big donors and having these big, fancy dinners, as if he cannot relate to the American people."

Meanwhile, Trump has turned his blame toward candidates he previously endorsed.

"If Greg Abbott, the Governor of Texas, hadn't become a RINO in the last six months of his Political Life, he wouldn't have lost," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "He went back to his original formula, and it wasn't pretty!"

Trump also blamed Fox News in a series of posts on Truth Social.

"Fox News bears responsibility for these losses by constantly and consistently putting on the Dumocrat opposition and worse," one post reads, criticizing the network for having former New York Mayor Bill de Blasio on air.

articles.title: From Texas to Kansas, 6 stunning midterm results that upended the political map
articles.summary: Democrats flipped seven Senate seats in a 2026 midterm referendum on Trump, ousting Susan Collins and defeating Attorney General Ken Paxton.
articles.body:
The 2026 midterms have been dubbed a referendum on President Donald Trump, and voters have decided.

Republicans have lost their control of the House and Senate, with Democrats so far winning 54 Senate seats and flipping seven of those seats. Meanwhile, Republicans' slim House majority was wiped away, as Democrats have won 228 seats, flipping 25 seats, and Republicans are at 139 seats.

Here are the top six surprises from Tuesday's election night.

Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, was ousted from her seat by Democratic candidate Troy Jackson, a fifth-generation logger, who campaigned on abolishing ICE and establishing Medicare for All.

Jackson's victory marks the end of Collins' nearly three-decade tenure as a bipartisan moderate. Collins previously broke ranks with Republicans on major votes such as Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill, the effort to repeal the Affordable Care Act and Trump's second impeachment trial.

She is Maine's longest-serving member of Congress and chaired the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee, a position that gave her significant influence over federal spending and funding for Maine projects.

Meanwhile, Jackson, who has been involved in Maine politics since the 2000s, entered the campaign in July after former Democratic nominee Graham Platner dropped out of the race following allegations of sexual assault, which he denied. Platner's campaign was riddled with controversy for months, following old Reddit posts from an account belonging to him in which he made disparaging remarks about poor White people and referred to himself as a "communist." He also faced criticism for a tattoo that resembled a Nazi symbol.

Abdul El-Sayed won the swing state of Michigan, becoming the first Muslim to be elected to the Senate.

The former Detroit Health Department leader faced pushback from a coalition of Jewish voters and Democrats concerned about his rhetoric on Israel and his ties to controversial political streamer Hasan Piker.

In his victory speech, El-Sayed invoked the Arabic phrase "alhamdulillah," which means "praise be to God."

The progressive candidate also issued a warning shot to his defeated opponent, former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers.

"Enjoy your retirement," El-Sayed said of the Republican candidate. "You chose hate, and Michigan chose hope. May we never have to see the likes of you in this state again."

El-Sayed ran his campaign on a two-point agenda, consisting of Medicare for All and getting corporate dollars out of politics. While not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), El-Sayed campaigned with socialist heavyweights, including Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt.

Meanwhile, Rogers was joined by President Donald Trump on the campaign trail, who warned that an El-Sayed victory would be detrimental to the country.

"If Abdul and the Democrats win, they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadis to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas," Trump said at a rally last month.

Republican Gov. Greg Abbott of Texas lost his re-election bid to Democratic candidate Gina Hinojosa, a state representative, ending his more than a decade in office.

"It has been the joy of my life to be the governor of the state of Texas," Abbott said to a crowd of supporters.

His defeat followed years of delivering key conservative priorities, including the nation's largest school voucher program, expansions of gun rights, stronger border enforcement, restrictions on abortion access and major property tax cuts. With affordability top of mind for voters, Abbott centered his re-election campaign on ensuring the cost of living remained low in Texas.

Meanwhile, Hinojosa framed the race as a fight against an affordability crisis being fueled by "the billionaires and the corporations," a message that carried her to victory and ended 36 years of Republican control of the governor's office.

Her key campaign promises included implementing moratoriums on data centers, rolling back the tax breaks Abbott gave to data centers and ending the school voucher program.

"Everything is bigger in Texas, including the shock of this win," Hinojosa said to a crowd of supporters. "We shocked the world tonight. With a Texas chip on our shoulder, we show that anything is possible."

Meanwhile, President Donald Trump, who has been an ally of Abbott since 2016, blamed Abbott for losing his seat on X.

"If Greg Abbott, the Governor of Texas, hadn't become a RINO in the last six months of his Political Life, he wouldn't have lost," Trump wrote. "He went back to his original formula, and it wasn't pretty!"

James Talarico will become the first Democratic senator to represent the Lone Star State in close to 40 years, defeating Texas Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, who was backed by Trump.

The upset comes as national Republicans and supporting PACs poured hundreds of millions of dollars into Paxton's campaign .

Trump and Paxton sought to portray Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian, as a far-left candidate, targeting his support for transgender minors and labeling him a "communist." Trump also dubbed him "Talafreako."

Paxton's defeat comes as Trump took a gamble in endorsing him a week before the May runoff race against incumbent Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas.

Trump dubbed Paxton a "true MAGA Warrior," and said Cornyn was a "good man," but said the incumbent was not always behind him when "times were tough."

Darline Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham , R-S.C., lost her election bid to Democratic challenger Annie Andrews, a pediatrician.

Andrews' victory marks the first time a Democrat has been elected to represent South Carolina in the U.S. Senate since 1998.

The loss came despite two Trump campaign appearances and Graham's name recognition as Lindsey Graham's sister. Her brother has held the office since 2003.

"She's smart and incredible. She'll never let you down," Trump said as he praised Darline at an Oct. 21 stop in Upstate South Carolina.

After Lindsey passed away in July, Gov. Henry McMaster appointed his sister to fill out the remainder of the late senator's current term, which concludes at the end of this year.

Lindsey had already won his primary race, so Darline ran in the special election following encouragement from Trump.

Democratic strategist Mally Smith told Fox News Digital that "South Carolina bows to no king."

"President Trump tried to handpick his successor in South Carolina, and the voters emphatically rejected his choice. Americans are sick of electing MAGA puppets to higher office who enable Trump's erratic behavior and blatant corruption," said Smith.

A Democratic candidate won the U.S. Senate seat for Kansas for the first time in 94 years, as megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton defeated first-term Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan.

Prior to the election, Marshall shared with Fox News Digital that he predicted if he wasn't able to win his re-election bid, then he believed Republicans wouldn't be able to maintain control of the Senate.

"I think that, you know, I'm not a political expert, I'm a physician, but if we lose Kansas, I don't see how we keep control of the Senate," Marshall told Fox News Digital in an interview before the election.

And Marshall's pre-election prediction came true as Democrats reclaimed control of the Senate.

Political strategists have said Hamilton's name recognition as the leader of the largest United Methodist church helped him in the state, while Marshall remained closely aligned with Trump, who joined him twice on the campaign trail weeks before the election.

"He was able to bring Republicans, independents and Democrats together to pull a stunning upset. The combination of a blue environment, a scandal-plagued incumbent and a strong Democrat like Hamilton made this upset possible," Democratic strategist Mally Smith said of Hamilton to Fox News Digital.

articles.title: How big money lost the 2026 midterms
articles.summary: Elon Musk’s record midterm spending and Vivek Ramaswamy’s run for Ohio governor both failed on election night, and the AI buildout now faces its own politica...
articles.body:
After the presidential election exactly two years ago, Elon Musk and Vivek Ramaswamy rode into Washington as protagonists of a new type of politics, running the short-lived Department of Government Efficiency. Last night, both suffered the worst defeats of their political careers.

Musk had moved many of his businesses to Texas and spent more than $200 million to hold the state for Republicans — part of a 2026 blitz that dwarfs any political spending by a single donor in a single election cycle — with returns that were diminishing, if not outright negative. Senate candidate Ken Paxton's numbers faded the more Musk spent. Ramaswamy lost his bid for Ohio governor, where his Republican predecessor won four years ago by 25 points, a bigger swing than can be explained by Trump's unpopularity and the blue wave that crested nearly everywhere.

The two seemed to embody a new type of hard-edged conservative politics that lives at the intersection of Twitter and money, driven by wealthy and successful businessmen who believed their wealth and success would translate into political victories and personal popularity.

I watched last night's results from Ramaswamy's gloomy election night party at an upscale Marriott in Columbus, Ohio, where a prayer circle was going in the women's bathroom by 9:45 pm. The outcomes suggest that money and its purest embodiments will be forced to slip politely back behind the curtain, to support more relatable public figures. Ramaswamy's fellow anti-woke traveler and fringe Wall Streeter, James Fishback, lost even earlier, in the primaries for Florida governor.

The biggest money in American corporate history — the huge new investments in AI — also had a hard night, as Trump's embrace of the technology helped doom his party. Now they have to find new ways to recast their projects as pro-worker and community-friendly to make sure the AI buildout actually happens — and to find spokespeople more appealing than the DOGE twins.

Shares in Musk's Tesla and SpaceX slide about 5% in pre-market trading Wednesday after Democrats won in Texas, where both companies are headquartered.
