articles.title: Trump redistricting push falls short as Dems hold GOP midterm targets
articles.summary: Democrats have won 11 seats in redrawn districts as of Wednesday.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Republicans only won two of the 15 U.S. House seats they aimed to gain through newly redrawn district maps in this year's midterm election.

The push by President Donald Trump saw Republicans spend the year approving new congressional maps, but many of the seats the GOP hoped to flip turned blue despite those efforts.

Democrats have won 11 seats in redrawn districts as of Wednesday. Democrats also won all six seats they were positioned to gain from new maps, including five in California redrawn in response to Trump's efforts and one in Utah , which was court-ordered.

The results arrived as NewsNation election partner Decision Desk HQ projected Democrats would control both the House and Senate.

Republicans' biggest setback came in Texas, where Trump said the party was "entitled" to five more seats. Republicans ultimately won one of the five seats and lost two they already held.

In Florida , Republicans targeted four Democratic seats but did not win any. Republicans did, however, gain seats in north Texas and Tennessee.

Redistricting in Louisiana , Alabama , Ohio and Utah were not the result of Trump's push. Courts also blocked Missouri's new map for this election. Virginia's Supreme Court struck down Democrats' redrawn map after it was approved by voters, which could have added four Democratic seats.

How many House seats did the GOP gain from redistricting?

The GOP has won two seats so far, which could rise if Republicans win a runoff in Louisiana — the state's House races were delayed due to a legal battle over redistricting.

How does a wave election flip gerrymandered seats?

Republicans built their maps around Trump's 2024 results, and many Texas targets relied on Latino voters who had moved toward him, but many of those voters backed Democrats this year, resulting in a blue wave.

Redrawing maps can weaken incumbency advantage

Sitting members of Congress often have an edge because voters are more familiar with them, but new lines can disrupt that relationship by adding voters who don't know them. About 71% of voters in Tennessee's new 9th District were new to it , according to Reuters.

Did mid-decade redistricting create a 'dummymander?'

A "dummymander" is a map drawn to help a party that ends up hurting it, often because the party spread its voters too thin, so they can't decide any single race. Trump's redrawn maps spread conservative supporters across more districts, which is sometimes referred to as "cracking" a district.

The push added seats but did not protect the GOP's House majority.

articles.title: Democrats usher in a new era with their resounding sweep of the House and the Senate
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrats are riding their sweep of Congress into a new era, eager to meet voter demands for change with plans to tackle high costs of livi...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrats are riding their sweep of Congress into a new era, eager to meet voter demands for change with plans to tackle high costs of living and confront President Donald Trump's final years in the White House.

In a nationwide romp, Democrats ousted Republicans from coast to coast , with many surprising places in between, as voters rejected the president's party for the promise of something different for the country. Their majorities will be padded by wide margins in both the House and the Senate.

The results set up a divided government, with Congress poised to reassert itself as a coequal branch ready to challenge Trump and reverse course after two years of unified GOP control.

"We hear you," said House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who would make history as the first Black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job when the new Congress begins on Jan. 3, 2027.

"We're going to work hard to deliver on the dramatic change that you deserve," he said.

The tally was decisive, at times bewildering, for the staggering scope of Democratic gains and the depth of Republican losses. The swelling margins underlined a deep sense of voter anger and concern over the economy and the state of democracy .

All told, the results present a fundamental reshaping of power in Washington, with new opportunities and challenges for governing.

Vice President JD Vance blamed war in Iran for Republican midterm losses.

Trump struck a conciliatory tone, suggesting he could work with the Democrats, but he also warned of gridlock ahead as he threatened to use the power of the presidential veto to strike down their agenda.

"I don't want to be just sitting there for two years vetoing everything," he told Politico.

House Speaker Mike Johnson will not seek reelection as House Republican leader following the Democrats' win, according to two people familiar with his plans who insisted on anonymity to disclose them.

Democrats vow a 100-day agenda and investigations of Trump

House Democrats are promising a 100-day agenda starting with efforts to lower the costs of gas, groceries and other goods, as well as bills to reverse cuts to the Affordable Care Act and Medicaid healthcare programs. They're also ready to launch a robust oversight agenda to, as Jeffries says, "hold the crooks accountable."

Impeachment — of the president or his Cabinet members — is an option.

The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, Rep. Robert Garcia of California, issued a one-sentence warning: "Lawyer up."

Sen. Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, issued his own one-word missive: "Subpoenas."

Democrats will be under pressure to quickly show that they have solutions for the high gas and grocery prices , the war in Iran and concerns about the direction of the country.

For Jeffries and his leadership team, it will be their first time in the majority, managing a class of newcomers including a handful of far-left democratic socialists .

With the majority in the 435-member House well past the 218 needed and the Senate Democrats holding at least 54 of 100 seats in that chamber, Jeffries and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer will have room to maneuver.

"Five words for the American people: Relief is on the way," the New York senator said.

A lame-duck session and leadership elections await Republicans

For Republicans, their shriveled numbers will create a reckoning of their own, as they try to figure out what went so uniformly wrong.

Johnson had quipped he may return to his Louisiana hometown of Shreveport to start a lawn care company if the Republicans lost power. Rivals seek to replace him.

Republicans may be anxious during the post-election lame-duck sprint to accomplish as much as possible in their remaining weeks in power. But hopes for another GOP-only priority package like their big tax breaks and spending cuts bill seem dim as defeated lawmakers prepare to go home at the end of the year.

Conservatives have also eyed the opportunity for Trump to nominate another justice to the Supreme Court while Senate Republicans still hold a majority. However, no current justice has announced any intent to step aside.

And the government could be headed toward a federal shutdown next month if Congress fails to pass a funding bill to keep operations running.

In the weeks ahead, the parties will hold internal leadership elections as members-elect arrive for freshman orientation at the Capitol.

The House will choose its speaker as one of the first votes when the new Congress convenes.

Vance cites the Iran war for Republicans' losses

In a lengthy online post, the vice president seemingly sought to distance himself from election results seen as a referendum on Trump that featured big Republican losses across the country.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote, adding, "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest."

Rarely has the president's party held on to power during midterm elections, but the Democratic sweep carried echoes of Trump's first term, when Republicans faced a voter revolt that sent Democrats to the House majority , and the Barack Obama era, when the Republican tea party swept to power.

This new Congress will also mark firsts and welcome trailblazers .

With the election of Democrat Julia Stratton of Illinois, the Senate will for the first time have three Black women in office.

Democrat Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota will be the first Native American female senator, Chris Pappas of New Hampshire will become the first openly gay male U.S. senator and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan will be the first Muslim to serve in the U.S. Senate .

Associated Press writers Tom Beaumont, Joey Cappelletti, Jill Colvin, Kevin Freking, Mary Clare Jalonick and Will Weissert contributed to this report.

Follow the AP's coverage of the 2026 elections at .

articles.title: Obama reacts to Democrats' landslide in midterm elections
articles.summary: Former President Barack Obama is reacting to Democrats' commanding victories in the midterm elections.
articles.body:
Former President Barack Obama said Americans sent a "clear message" in the midterm elections after Democrats swept major races across the country and won control of Congress .

"Tonight, the American people sent a clear message — they want a politics that brings people together rather than divides them, and leaders who offer concrete solutions to the challenges they face," he said in a social media statement .

Democrats prevailed in a landslide, flipping dozens of seats in a sharp repudiation of President Donald Trump and the GOP.

The candidates Obama backed ahead of midterms – including Abdul El-Sayed , Amy Acton and Keisha Lance Bottoms – prevailed over their Republican opponents in their respective Senate and gubernatorial campaigns.

Obama's return to the campaign trail in recent weeks made headlines as he blasted Trump's first two years in office . He even likened the White House decor to that of a Cheesecake Factory and made a rare mention of his tan suit controversy .

Obama rallies Atlanta voters with Ossoff and Bottoms at Georgia event

Obama on midterm election results: 'Our job now is to roll up our sleeves'

Obama credited winning candidates in areas once considered long shots.

"They came from different backgrounds and represented a range of political perspectives, but were united by shared values, a belief in public service, and a commitment to putting the people of their districts and states first," Obama said.

In Texas, James Talarico will be the first Democratic Texas senator in more than three decades, while Troy Jackson defeated five-term Republican Sen. Susan Collins in Maine.

But Democrats have to continue riding the blue wave into the next two years, Obama added.

"While this administration has another two years in office, our job now is to roll up our sleeves, make changes wherever we have the power to do so, prevent further damage, and lay the groundwork for the future," he said.

Obama's headline-making moments on midterms campaign trail

As candidates rallied voters in the final few weeks before midterm elections, Obama joined several on the campaign trail, even at times drawing ire from Trump .

During an Oct. 24 rally in Michigan to back El-Sayed , the former president said Trump's renovation projects – like the controversial White House ballroom and the paved over Rose Garden – make the White House look "like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory."

Republicans seized on the comment as a sign of elitism, while Trump called Obama "a lousy president." Obama later responded that the restaurant chain was "my jam for about a decade."

The former president also evoked a notorious fashion scandal from his White House stint. While campaigning at an Oct. 28 rally in Georgia for Jon Ossoff and Lance Bottoms , Obama revisited his controversial tan suit .

"I'm old enough to remember when a president wearing a tan suit was a major national controversy," he told the crowd . "They were very upset. And I know I looked good in the suit."

Melina Khan is a national trending reporter for USA TODAY. Keep up with her on Instagram @bymelinakhan and TikTok @melina.khan2 .

articles.title: Massie: Midterm results ‘about holding Republicans accountable for betraying their promises’
articles.summary: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), who has bucked his party in recent years, said Tuesday’s midterm blowout by Democrats was “about holding Republicans accountable...
articles.body:
Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), who has bucked his party in recent years, said Tuesday's midterm blowout by Democrats was "about holding Republicans accountable for betraying their promises."

"Tonight's outcome isn't about placing faith in Democrats or socialist principles; it's about holding Republicans accountable for betraying their promises," Massie said Tuesday night on the social platform X .

"All Republicans had to do was: 1. put Americans First 2. not start another war 3. prosecute sex traffickers," he added.

A blue wave swept across the U.S. on Tuesday, with the Democrats winning both the House and Senate majorities and securing a chance of restricting President Trump's power until the end of his second term.

The Democrats' victories came amid rocky political territory for the GOP, with Republicans weighed down by issues including the unpopular war in Iran, President Trump's slumping approval numbers and concerns about the cost of living.

Democrats are projected to end up with 257 seats in the House and 55 seats in the Senate , according to Decision Desk HQ, marking gains for the party that currently holds 214 seats in the lower chamber and 45 seats in the upper.

In September, Massie, who lost his primary to an opponent supported by Trump, predicted a backlash toward the president and his party in this year's midterm elections.

"I think his comeuppance will happen on Election Day, and the day after I think there's going to be a reckoning," Massie, who has been a vocal critic of Trump and his policies, told CNN's Kaitlan Collins at the time.

Massie has crossed the aisle to back multiple Iran war powers resolutions and spearheaded a bipartisan effort for the release of files linked to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

articles.title: James Talarico ends 30 years of GOP dominance in Texas Senate race
articles.summary: Democrat James Talarico defeated Ken Paxton to win a U.S. Senate seat, ending decades of GOP control in Texas.
articles.body:
For the first time in three decades, Texas voters bucked single-party rule and elected Democrat James Talarico to serve in the U.S. Senate, sending a clear message to Republicans that they are ready for a change in policies and a change in discourse.

Unofficial election night results showed Talarico toppling former Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton by a significant margin, prompting the Associated Press and CNN to call the race with only about 27% of Texas polling locations reporting on election night.

The stunning, historic and decisive victory was more than enough to secure his place as the replacement for outgoing U.S. Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who likely would have been a shoo-in for Republicans had he not lost in the May runoff to one of the most corrupt politicians to ever come out of the Lone Star State.

"We just took back Texas," Talarico said from his election night watch party in Austin. "We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas. We just showed that a politics of division is no match for a politics of love. And we just sent a message to every billionaire megadonor, every trillionaire megadonor, every corrupt defender of this broken political system in this state, in this country, power belongs to the people."

The victory for Talarico was far from an isolated incident as Texas truly experienced a blue wave with Democrat Gina Hinojosa toppling incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott and other Democrats winning statewide up and down the ballot.

After his historic victory, Talarico appeared behind a "Love Thy Neighbor" campaign sign, underscoring a key theme of his campaign.

Raised a Presbyterian and a theology student who put seminary school on hold while he pursued the U.S. Senate seat, Talarico made his faith a central part of his campaign and shifted gears from the dogmatic, evangelical Christian standard to a fresh perspective where love, charity and grace were more than religious ideals; they became political positions that can be acted on to improve the lives of everyday Texans.

Talarico was able to build on a groundswell of frustration with President Donald Trump 's "America First" agenda, which over the last two years has saddled Americans with sky-high prices for groceries and other basic necessities because of unneeded tariffs, increased the price of gas by more than a dollar because of an unpopular war in Iran, and injected a vitriol into American politics that has done the type of damage that will likely take decades to repair.

And unlike his opponent, Talarico's campaign did not rely on megadonors like Elon Musk, who injected hundreds of millions of dollars into Texas races in a bid to keep Trump and his ilk in power, it was a campaign built around everyday Texans backing a relatively unknown state legislator with a dream of unifying Texans.

To be sure, Talarico has an uphill battle as he prepares to take his place in the upper chamber of Congress — the Trump agenda still dominates Washington and Democrats will have to avoid the veto pen to enact any meaningful legislation — but he will be a key piece of his party's attempts to buck Trump and Republicans for the next two years.

Talarico was virtually unknown outside of Texas when he launched his U.S. Senate campaign in September 2025.Before becoming a member of the Texas House of Representatives, Talarico worked as a public-school teacher in San Antonio, where his work with at-risk and low-income students inspired him to consider a career in politics.He was first elected to the Texas House in 2018 at the age of 29 — during his four-year tenure in the Republican-controlled legislature, he served as lead author on more than 200 bills, 16 of which were signed into law. Much of his legislative action was aimed at education and childcare, but his bill capping the price of insulin was possible his landmark work in the Texas Legislature.

When he launched his U.S. Senate campaign, Talarico entered a contentious battle against U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Dallas, who was well-known among Democratic voters and party elites and widely expected to win the March 2026 Democratic primary.

But Talarico quickly gained steam in the contest with multiple newspaper endorsements and an appearance on "The View," which sparked a Federal Communications Commission (FCC) investigation and added to Talarico's growing popularity. He ran afoul of the FCC again when he appeared on an episode of "The Late Show with Stephen Colbert" that was broadcast online due to Trump's increased pressure on television networks, especially those promoting Democrats.

The publicity quickly made Talarico a household name well beyond Texas and on March 3 he bested Crockett to advance to the November General Election, which at that time was still a shakeup between Attorney General Ken Paxton and incumbent U.S. Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas.

Despite his myriad failings as a viable candidate and doubts among political observers that he could best a populist candidate like Talarico, Paxton won the May Republican primary runoff , ending Cornyn's time in Washington and setting up the Nov. 3 showdown with Talarico.

The campaign between May and November proved to be a scorched earth effort on both sides — Paxton sought to paint Talarico as a radical extremist opposed to traditional Texas values, while Talarico leaned on Paxton's various scandals during his time as attorney general.

The attacks on Talarico proved to hold little water, however, as even Republicans began flocking to his side, unable to even hold their noses and cast a ballot for Paxton, whose campaign lagged significantly behind Talarico's in terms of energy, activity and fundraising, especially in the final days of the campaign.By Election Day, Paxton's campaign appeared dead on arrival and Talarico's star was only beginning to shine.

Throughout his U.S. Senate campaign, Talarico has left little doubt on where he stands on the biggest issues facing Texans, as well as those plaguing the rest of the United States, such as a growing affordability crisis, underfunded public schools, stagnant wages, a dysfunctional immigration system and ongoing conflicts in the Middle East. All of those priorities will certainly be front of mind for Talarico as he prepares to be sworn into the U.S. Senate on Jan. 3, 2027.

A key platform for Talarico throughout the campaign was eliminating the impact of wealthy donors on American politics, a scourge that has corrupted the country's political system since the landmark Citizens United ruling, which allowed corporations to spend unlimited amounts to influence elections.

Along with refusing corporate PAC money since his 2017 campaign, Talarico's plan for the U.S. Senate includes banning partisan gerrymandering nationwide, prohibiting stock trading by Congress, implementing congressional term limits and reversing the Citizens United ruling.

On the economic front, Talarico's "New American Dream" plan includes repealing tax cuts for the wealthiest 1% of Americans, universal childcare and paid family leave, closing tax loopholes for billionaires, expanding the Child Tax Credit and Earned Income Tax Credit and repealing Trump's tariffs, a major catalyst for the rising cost of groceries in the United States.

Talarico also has a slew of ambitious plans: he hopes to lower the cost of health care by allowing every American, regardless of age, to join Medicare and reversing Trump's disastrous cuts to Affordable Care Act (ACA) subsidies; he aims to take on big tech by ensuring data centers fund their own infrastructure upgrades rather than passing costs onto local consumers and giving citizens a cut of AI profit growth; and he looks to advance comprehensive immigration reform that includes holding ICE accountable for abuses, creating pathways to legal citizenship for some undocumented immigrants and overhauling the nation's beleaguered asylum system.

"This is a win the size of Texas," Talarico said on election night. "And now we have a mandate the size of Texas. This election was about chasing a vision of what this state can be: Texas public schools that are the envy of the nation; a Texas economy that is second to none; and Texas families that are stronger and healthier than they've ever been."

"It won't happen overnight," he added. "But a giant state deserves giant dreams."

articles.title: Was it a blue tsunami? Explaining Democrats' major midterms gains
articles.summary: Democrats are projected to retake control of the Senate and House of Representatives from Republicans.
articles.body:
Democrats are poised to retake control of the Senate and House of Representatives after a string of victories, or upsets, across the country on Election Day in what political pundits are calling not just a "blue wave," but a " blue tsunami ."

The term refers to a wave election in which a political party makes significant gains, whether that is Democrats, represented by blue or Republicans, represented by red. The 2026 midterm election on Nov. 3 saw major swings toward the Democratic party.

With Democrats snatching control of Congress, the legislative branch is poised to become a much bigger thorn in President Donald Trump's side. Here's what to know.

Byron Donalds celebrates historic victory as Florida’s first Black governor

A "blue wave" or "blue tsunami" refers to an election where the Democratic Party – represented by the color blue – makes major gains across the country. Republicans faced losses in red states and districts that Trump had carried by double digits just two years ago.

The opposite, where the Republican party makes major gains, is similarly called a red wave.

According to USA Facts , the United States saw a big red wave in the 2010 midterms when Republicans gained 64 House seats and six Senate seats from the previous election. The site notes a large blue wave occurred in 2018 when Democrats won 41 additional House seats despite ceding one in the Senate.

What Democratic wins lead to a blue wave?

The Democratic Party swept races across Texas, Iowa, Ohio, South Carolina and Kansas, which hadn't elected a Democratic senator since 1932 . Democrats are also projected to flip several Republican-held House seats from Indiana to Tennessee. In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed beat his Republican opponent Mike Rogers to become the nation's first Muslim senator.

The blue wave has also included gubernatorial races, which saw Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms win in Georgia and Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeat Gov. Greg Abbott in Texas.

Two Senate races − in Alaska and Mississippi − remain undecided. GOP Sens. Daniel S. Sullivan and Cindy Hyde-Smith, respectively, were each ahead early Nov. 4, but the races were too close to call. The Justice Department has appealed a lawsuit to investigate the Alaska results if the incumbent, Sullivan, loses by a small enough margin that a challenger with the same name made the difference.

Even with Republicans in the majority, Congress has become increasingly willing to rebuke Trump over the past year.

Both chambers have voted to end the war in Iran and release the Epstein files. The House has repudiated Trump's tariffs on Canada while outgoing GOP senators pushed back on Trump's plans to build a White House ballroom and launch an "anti-weaponization" fund.

But Republican leadership had largely worked to advance Trump's agenda. With Democrats poised to take over, that's about to change.

Trump responded to the Democratic rout by stating in a social media post that Republicans would have won had he been on the ballot, even though the race was largely seen as a referendum on his second term.

The president told the New York Times that he is "absolutely willing to accept" the election results.

"We'll work with the Democrats, and we'll, you know, look forward to working with them. We'll probably work something out," Trump said.

Trump also indicated that the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran likely played a role in his party's defeat in the midterms, Reuters reported .

"Iran was a piece of it," he told The Wall Street Journal, per Reuters.

And while his campaign promises "no new wars," Trump stood by his decision to attack Iran.

"I did the right thing," he said in his interview with the Wall Street Journal. "I would have done it again."

Contributing: Bart Jansen, Erin Mansfield and Zachary Schermele, USA TODAY

articles.title: Five reasons why Republicans lost so badly
articles.summary: From angry voters to an unpopular president, here is why Americans in traditional Republican areas turned to Democrats.
articles.body:
The Democrats have swept to victory in the US midterm elections, taking control of Congress.

While the incumbent president's party generally tends to have a bad night in these elections, the scale of the Republican defeat is being viewed as a resounding rejection of Donald Trump's two years in the White House.

From angry voters to an unpopular president , here are five reasons why the Republicans lost so many seats .

From coast to coast, voters across the US have been grappling with the soaring cost of essentials. That anger was palpable on the ground in key races.

"Gas prices, grocery prices, everything's going up," one North Carolina voter told the BBC ahead of the elections, adding that she had switched her vote from Republican to Democratic this election.

Prices increased by 3.7% in the year to September, driven higher by fuel and energy prices. Average US retail diesel prices in early October were just shy of the record of $6.52 (£4.83) per gallon seen in September, according to government data.

Almost eight in 10 voters (79%) said inflation had caused them and their family a severe or moderate hardship in the past year, according to data from voter polls.

And more than six in 10 respondents laid the blame for that at the feet of Trump, saying they thought higher than usual prices were because of the president's policies.

A major factor in surging prices has been the war with Iran which the US and Israel launched in February.

Fuel prices then shot up after Tehran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation, strangling a key artery for the passage of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG).

US voters have been paying the price at the petrol pump ever since.

The war has proved broadly unpopular with most Americans. For Maga Republicans it also felt like a broken promise in Trump's America First campaign agenda in which he pledged there would be no more wars .

Around six in 10 (63%) of those asked in a voter poll said the US made the wrong decision to take military action against Iran.

Separately, three-quarters of voters (74%) said the conflict was a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress.

The morning after the election, Trump conceded the war had played a role in the defeat but insisted in an interview on Fox that he had no choice but to intervene to stop Iran getting a nuclear weapon.

The scale and breadth of this Democratic wave was made possible by some strong candidates who came across as authentic, especially in traditional Republican heartlands.

They stuck to a disciplined message about the cost of living and healthcare access.

Former teacher James Talarico and pastor Adam Hamilton also talked about their faith in a way that struck a chord in Texas and Kansas respectively.

In South Carolina, Democrat Annie Andrews pulled off a shock upset. A former paediatrician, her focus on health care affordability resonated in a country where many see the system as broken.

Former public health official Abdul El-Sayed, who triumphed in Michigan to keep that seat Democratic, made getting "money out of politics, money in your pocket" a key slogan.

Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, who won re-election in Georgia, made the cost of living and corruption a central message. The 39-year-old's comfortable victory in a state Trump won twice will only fuel rumours of a 2028 presidential run.

Even Trump himself praised the Democrats, telling Fox News they "did a good job".

Conversely, some Republican candidates like Ken Paxton in Texas were criticised for running poor campaigns that were not focused enough on voters' concerns.

4. Trump's unpopularity a drag on Republicans

Two of the issues voters were most unhappy with - rocketing prices and the Iran War - were directly linked to the president.

His approval ratings had even fallen among Republican voters, which made some of these states which backed him in 2024 especially vulnerable.

He urged voters to imagine he was on the ballot in an effort to galvanise his supporters.

But after more than a decade as the central figure in American politics, some see these results as evidence that the glitz may be wearing off Trump's brand.

Against a backdrop of increasing anger, making himself the focus of the Republican campaign was risky and appears to have backfired .

In the months leading up to the vote, polling indicated that many Americans wanted Trump to focus more on their concerns about rocketing prices.

In his final campaign speech on Monday in Washington DC, he talked at length about his controversial renovation project of the Reflecting Pool behind him.

5. Hispanic and black voters shift again

Two years ago a move towards Republicans among some Hispanic and black voters helped Trump secure a decisive win. That seems to have reversed in these midterms.

Democrats claimed all three House races in the overwhelmingly Hispanic congressional districts along the Texas-Mexico border.

Majority-Hispanic counties moved more than 22 percentage points against Republican Senate candidates, compared with the 2024 presidential election, according to a New York Times analysis.

The change is more than any other major demographic group in the country, data reporter Jeff Adelson said.

The shift comes amid widespread anger at immigration enforcement, with a majority (56%) of Americans saying they have an unfavourable opinion of ICE, according to the Pew Research Center.

Counties with a black majority also moved significantly towards Democratic candidates in Senate races.

The Senate race is on a knife-edge in Mississippi, which has the largest share of black voters of any US state with around 37%.

If Scott Colom can win, he would become the first Democrat elected to the Senate in Mississippi since 1982.

articles.title: The biggest races Democrats won in the midterms
articles.summary: Democrats won pivotal races in Texas, South Carolina, Georgia, Michigan and elsewhere. Here are the biggest victories of the 2026 midterms.
articles.body:
Washington — Voters across the country delivered a stinging rebuke to Republicans in Congress and President Trump's agenda in the 2026 midterm elections on Tuesday, with Democrats capturing House and Senate seats that had seemed out of reach just a few months ago.

CBS News projects Democrats will take control of both chambers when the new Congress convenes in January, with wide margins in each. Democrats are projected to control at least 54 Senate seats, with two races still unresolved. In the House , CBS News estimates the party could control between 251 and 268 when all the votes are counted.

Out of 11 Senate races that CBS News considered battlegrounds, Democrats were projected to win 10. The 11th race, in Alaska, is still rated a toss-up as results come in. The Mississippi Senate race is also unresolved and is unexpectedly close, with Democrat Scott Colom leading incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by just 43 votes. CBS News has rated that race as a toss-up.

The victories weren't just limited to House and Senate races, either. Democrats captured the governor's mansion in Texas, a feat they haven't accomplished since 1990.

Here are the major races that propelled Democrats to victory on Tuesday, according to CBS News' projections:

Hinojosa, a state lawmaker, bested Republican incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott , making her the first Democrat to win the governor's mansion in more than 30 years. Hinojosa will be the third woman to lead the state.

Abbott had been in office for more than a decade and was seeking a fourth term as governor, and the race against Hinojosa narrowed in the months leading up to the election. Hinojosa focused her campaign on affordability and public education. The fight over data centers also emerged as a major issue in the governor's race.

Andrews, a pediatrician, defeated Republican Sen. Darline Graham , the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham. Andrews, 45, made healthcare access and affordability the focuses of her campaign.

Graham was appointed to finish out the remainder of her late brother's Senate term following his unexpected death in July. President Trump swiftly threw his support behind Graham and campaigned for her in South Carolina in the lead-up to the midterms.

It has been nearly 30 years since a Democrat won the Senate in South Carolina, a state Mr. Trump won by 18 points in 2024.

Hamilton, a fifth-generation Kansan, is the leader of the largest United Methodist church in the country and is a well-known author and speaker. The 62-year-old defeated Roger Marshall, a Republican, who was seeking his second term in the Senate.

Kansas hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932. Mr. Trump won the state by more than 16 points in the last presidential election.

In the closing weeks of the Senate campaign, Marshall, an obstetrician-gynecologist, came under scrutiny after the New York Times reported that he had filed lawsuits against hundreds of his patients over outstanding medical bills, and 81 were arrested.

In the most expensive Senate race in Texas history, and one of the closest-watched matchups of the election cycle, Talarico defeated Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton .

Talarico, 37, is a former teacher and Presbyterian seminarian who was elected to serve in the Texas House of Representatives in 2018.

Talarico's campaign focused on corruption and lowering costs. He told "CBS Mornings" on Wednesday that his victory sent a message to Elon Musk, who spent heavily in the race, that "Texas is not for sale."

"The power in this state, in this country, belongs to the people and we've got to make sure it stays that way," he said.

Paxton was backed by Mr. Trump, who endorsed the Republican attorney general over Sen. John Cornyn in the GOP Senate primary earlier this year.

Paxton went on to defeat Cornyn in the primary runoff in May, setting the race against Talarico. Paxton had weathered numerous controversies and was impeached by the state House in 2023 on allegations of bribery, obstruction of justice and abuse of trust. He was acquitted by the state Senate.

In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms will make history as the nation's first Black woman governor. The former Atlanta mayor and senior adviser in the Biden administration defeated Republican Rick Jackson and Libertarian Chase Oliver, CBS News projects.

With 99% of the vote counted, Bottoms had 54.3% of the vote, compared to 45.7% for Jackson.

Bottoms told "CBS Mornings" on Wednesday that she was surprised that the race was called as early as it was on election night.

"I thought that it was going to be a very long night. I knew that we had done the work, but Georgia has always, for the past few years, been a purple state, so I thought it would be much closer," she said.

Michigan was viewed as Republicans' best chance to flip a Senate seat, but El-Sayed's victory over GOP opponent Mike Rogers keeps it in Democrats' hands.

The Senate race emerged as one of the most contentious of the midterm election cycle. Top Republicans, led by Mr. Trump, repeatedly leveled anti-Muslim attacks against El-Sayed , calling him a "jihadist" and claiming that he is a member of the Muslim Brotherhood.

El-Sayed told Fox News in an interview last month that he has "never been a member of the Muslim Brotherhood."

El-Sayed also came under scrutiny for his opposition to U.S. support for Israel and views on Israel raising questions as to whether he could win support from Jewish and Black voters.

There was a late twist in the Senate race in Michigan when Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, who sought the Democratic Senate nomination, endorsed Rogers and appeared alongside him at a Detroit church Sunday.

Jackson was facing off against GOP Sen. Susan Collins , the only Republican running for reelection in a state won by former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential race.

Collins was first elected to represent Maine in the Senate in 1996 and had touted her ability to bring home benefits for the state as part of her pitch to voters. While she had survived difficult campaigns in the past, Collins was not able to fend off the challenge from Jackson.

Jackson is a fifth-generation logger who jumped into the Senate race late after Graham Platner, who initially won the Democratic Senate nomination, withdrew from the race after allegations of sexual misconduct. The former president of the Maine Senate unsuccessfully sought the Democratic nomination for governor earlier this year.

Dozens of House seats across the country

Democrats are on track to flip dozens of House seats.

In Iowa, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, Democrats had a sweep of the most competitive seats.

Democrats defeated GOP incumbent Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa, Zach Nunn of Iowa, Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, Ryan Mackenzie of Pennsylvania, Rob Bresnahan Jr. of Pennsylvania, Scott Perry of Pennsylvania, Brian Steil of Wisconsin and Derrick Van Orden of Wisconsin. They also flipped an open Iowa seat that is currently held by the GOP.

Redistricting helped Democrats win California's 1st District and Utah's 1st District. Redistricting was expected to hamper Democrats' chances in Texas' 15th District and 23rd District, but Democrats pulled off upsets.

In Ohio, embattled GOP Reps. Max Miller and Mike Carey both lost reelection, as did Tom Kean in New Jersey, Ann Wagner in Missouri, Gabe Evans in Colorado, Victoria Spartz in Indiana and Jen Kiggans in Virginia.

Democrats also flipped open seats in Kentucky's 6th District, Nebraska's 2nd District and North Carolina's 11th District.

articles.title: CBS News exit polls show how Democrats won in the midterms
articles.summary: Economic issues helped propel President Trump to victory in 2024, and those same issues dragged down his party in 2026.
articles.body:
Note: Poll percentages may have updated since this was published.

Economic issues helped propel President Trump to victory in 2024, and those same issues dragged down his party in 2026.

Fueled in part by economic frustration, parts of the Democratic coalition that Mr. Trump made inroads with in 2024 swung back toward Democrats this year.

Persistent negative views of the economy turned against the party in power. Those who said the economy was bad voted for Democrats for the House, according to CBS News exit polls.

This was the second straight election most voters told us inflation was a hardship for them, and more said their finances are worse now compared to two years ago — these voters backed Democrats over the Republicans for the House.

This election was clearly a referendum on Mr. Trump and largely a rejection of his policies.

Nationally, most said his tariffs hurt the economy, his administration's immigration efforts went too far and the decision to take military action against Iran was the wrong one.

In 2024, Mr. Trump made gains nationally with young voters, Latinos and women, but majorities of all these groups backed Democrats for the House this year. Democrats' margins with women were similar to what they were in 2018 when Democrats won control of the House during the president's first term.

And majorities of each of these key groups said the cost of living was crucial in their vote.

Democrats made inroads with Republican-leaning groups

Historically, men have generally backed Republicans in both presidential and midterm elections, but they largely split their votes this year.

Mr. Trump won men by double digits in 2024. Today, most disapprove of the job he is doing, and those who do backed Democrats.

White women historically mostly vote Republican, but they narrowly backed Democrats in this election, according to exit polls.

The national electorate was slightly more Democratic than the most recent two elections, which helped Democrats. But their lead with independents was critical in putting them over the top.

This electorate was a pessimistic one — unhappy about the state of the country and the economy and not very hopeful for the next generation.

So the Democrats may have their work cut out for them.

Just over half of voters had an unfavorable view of the party. Voters did give the Democrats an edge over Republicans on the economy, so they likely expect results.

Joe Williams contributed to this report.

The CBS News exit poll interviewed thousands of voters across the country at polling locations on Election Day and in the weeks leading up to Election Day. This is how the voter polling was conducted .

articles.title: Mississippi Senate race unresolved in surprisingly competitive contest
articles.summary: The Senate race in deep-red Mississippi remains unresolved Wednesday morning, as Democrat Scott Colom has mounted a surprisingly competitive challenge to inc...
articles.body:
Washington — The Senate midterm race in deep-red Mississippi remains unresolved Wednesday morning, with Democrat Scott Colom mounting a surprisingly competitive challenge to incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

With 96% of the vote in, just a few dozen votes separated the candidates, a stunningly close result in the Magnolia State.

Hyde-Smith, 67, has been in the Senate since 2018 and is seeking reelection. But Colom, a district attorney, launched a formidable challenge, and could deliver Democrats yet another victory.

Democrats saw a slew of wins in Senate races Tuesday night, including in states that President Trump won by double digits in the 2024 elections. With more than four flips of GOP-held seats, Democrats secured enough seats to take control of the chamber in the new year. If Colom manages to pull off a victory, he would add to their majority.

Colom, 43, is a seventh-generation Mississippian who campaigned on cost of living and health care issues. Democrats began investing in the race in recent weeks, seeing an opportunity for a pickup. But the possible outcome still appeared exceedingly unlikely heading into Election Day.

Mr. Trump won Mississippi by 20 points in 2024, and the state hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982.

Speaking to supporters in the wee hours of the morning on Wednesday, Colom said, "The results are all trending in our direction."

"We are trending in counties that people thought we had no chance to compete in," Colom said. "And we're winning them."

The unresolved race in Mississippi comes as Alaska's Senate race is also outstanding, leaving the size of Democrats' majority up in the air.

articles.title: Alaska Senate race unresolved, with weekslong process possible
articles.summary: The Senate race in Alaska, which has garnered widespread attention with two candidates named Dan Sullivan, remains in limbo.
articles.body:
Washington — The Senate race in Alaska remains unresolved Wednesday, as a contest that has garnered widespread attention over the two candidates named Dan Sullivan faces a lengthy ballot-counting process.

Incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola are facing off in the race, which also has two other candidates on the ballot: an independent candidate and retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan, and another Republican, Gerald Heikes.

With around three-quarters of the vote in as of Wednesday morning, the race remains a toss-up, according to CBS News estimates.

The count in Alaska could stretch on. Alaska has a ranked-choice voting system , which allows voters to rank as many or as few candidates as they'd like in order of preference. If no candidate secures support from more than 50% of voters as their top choice, the count goes to a second round.

The ranked-choice tabulation doesn't occur until the last counting of ballots 15 days after Election Day, meaning the process could drag on for weeks if one candidate does not secure more than 50% of first-place support on the ballot.

The results in Alaska will come after Democrats already secured enough seats to take control of the Senate , winning in several states that President Trump won by double digits in 2024. Alaska could either add to the Democrats' majority, or deliver some relief to Republicans by blunting additional Democratic gains. One other Senate contest, the Mississippi race , also remained unresolved Wednesday morning.

Speaking to reporters early Wednesday morning, Peltola said, "The results are not going to be fast."

"But Alaskans are patient," she said. "We just want to make sure the folks [in] the Lower 48 know it won't be hours, it won't be days, it will be weeks."

Sen. Sullivan likewise emphasized to supporters, "We're going to have a long night," adding, "We're probably going to have some long weeks."

articles.title: Ilhan Omar lashes out at 'bigot' Trump after winning re-election despite investigation
articles.summary: Ilhan Omar told supporters Democrats' midterm victories sent a message to Trump, as she addressed federal probes and Operation Metro Surge protests.
articles.body: After winning re-election on Tuesday, Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., told supporters early Wednesday that Democrats' overwhelming victories across the country sent a message to "the bigot in the White House and his friends that we are not going to be a pawn in their game." Omar referring to President Donald Trump as a "bigot" comes after his repeated attacks on the congresswoman whom he has called "garbage," a "disaster" and a "disgrace to our country." He has also said Omar, who became a U.S. citizen in 2000, should "go back" to Somalia. Omar won her race this cycle with more than 76% of the vote, continuing her string of landslide general election victories in one of the bluest congressional districts in the country. The two federal criminal investigations she faces — both of which became public just over three weeks before Election Day — did not appear to dissuade voters in Minnesota's 5th Congressional District from supporting her. ILHAN OMAR BELIEVES TRUMP RAID ON HOME WAS MEANT TO 'INTIMIDATE AND SCARE PEOPLE' FROM VOTING In her speech, Omar appeared to reference Operation Metro Surge, which deployed thousands of federal immigration officers primarily to Minneapolis and St. Paul to carry out removal operations. The operation drew fierce local opposition and large-scale protests, during which two protesters, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were killed. "When this administration came for Minnesotans, we knew that we could respond by showing up in the streets and protecting our neighbors, but we also knew when Election Day came that we were going to provide an answer by directly rejecting them in the ballot box," Omar said. Omar also addressed the federal probes examining whether she fraudulently obtained U.S. citizenship and whether there were discrepancies in her financial disclosures, framing them as an attempt by the White House to intimidate her and her supporters. 175 DEMOCRATS DEMAND TRUMP ADMIN STOP ILHAN OMAR INVESTIGATION, WARN IT COULD HURT HER RE-ELECTION BID "When they decided that they were going to come for me, they thought that they were going to find someone who was going to cower," Omar said. "They thought they were going to find a community that was going to live in fear. They thought that if you attacked me and you silenced me, that my community wouldn't show up and vote." Omar shouted out Democratic victories in the Ohio, Maine and Texas Senate races, arguing it proved there had been a backlash against the Trump administration's policies over the last two years. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP She concluded her remarks by echoing Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who said after the Democratic wave that the Trump family should "lawyer up." Come January, Garcia is set to become chairman of the House Oversight Committee, which has subpoena power to compel testimony and obtain documents. "He said, 'You better lawyer up.' Because your time of harassment is over. It is our time for accountability and transparency. And if you thought that the Democrats took it easy on you in 2019, wait until you meet these kind of new Democrats," Omar said.

articles.title: Opposition parties demand review of booth distribution
articles.summary: Opposition parties in Kolkata allege KMC ward delimitation map errors and booth mismatches, urging a review ahead of poll notification; CPM cites 100 booths needing changes.
articles.body: Kolkata: Opposition parties have flagged concerns about the way booths have been distributed among new wards of Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC).Both CPM and Congress have raised objections and demanded a review.Congress functionary Ashutosh Chatterjee, who attended a hearing on Wednesday in respect of draft rolls for KMC polls published last week, said the map that was being shown to them now was different from the map shown when hearings for revision of ward boundaries were conducted in KMC.“It has been found that during the delimitation process, we were called by the concerned hearing officers of KMC as per our objections, wherein wrong maps were, strangely, used for the hearing process. We want to know why such wrong maps were used to conduct such important hearings in relation to the delimitation exercise which result in fabrication,” Chatterjee wrote in a letter to Bengal’s CEO, state election commissioner (SEC) and KMC commissioner. “Such undemocratic means clearly depict that there was an intention behind such exercise for which we strongly object,” the letter said.A CPM functionary said nearly 100 booths need changes. “The booth distribution in the list handed over to us last week does not always match with the maps. The booth distribution is filled with errors. A voter from Tollygunge Phanri must go to Jodhpur Park to cast his vote. We have found about 100, out of 4,722 booths, that need changes,” said Subrata Dutta, CPM’s Kolkata district secretariat member.Poll officials said the 4,722 booths were distributed across 1,835 polling stations in the KMC area.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Kolkata | Silver Rate in Kolkata | Bank Holidays in Kolkata | Public Holidays in Kolkata | Kolkata AQI | Weather in Kolkata | Petrol Price in Kolkata | Diesel Price in Kolkata | CNG Price in Kolkata | LPG Price in KolkataStay updated with the latest Kolkata news. articles.title: Speaker Johnson won't seek reelection as House Republican leader after party's midterm wipeout
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — House Speaker Mike Johnson will be stepping aside from Republican Party leadership after the GOP’s wipeout in the midterm election, declini...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — House Speaker Mike Johnson will be stepping aside from Republican Party leadership after the GOP's wipeout in the midterm election , declining to seek support to stay on as House minority leader in the new Congress, according to two people familiar with his decision Wednesday.

Johnson is expected to retain his seat as a rank-and-file member of the House from Louisiana when the Congress convenes in January. He won reelection from his Shreveport-area district for an eighth term in office.

It's a swift rise and fall for Johnson, often seen as an accidental speaker, who nevertheless drew close to President Donald Trump and led the House GOP during a tumultuous era, with one of the slimmest majorities in modern times.

And it sets up a fierce internal party battle for the new GOP leader after Democrats swept to power.

Rep. Steve Scalise, the House majority leader, is running for the leadership post, according to a person familiar with his plans. The people who told The Associated Press about Johnson's and Scalise's decisions insisted on anonymity to disclose them.

House Republicans are expected to elect their new leader when members-elect gather in Washington next week, in what will likely be a familiar showdown between two who reached for the top spot before — Scalise of Louisiana and Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio.

Johnson's sunny assertions that Republicans would defy history in the midterms , as voters traditionally have punished the president's party in power, failed to hold. Instead, Republicans were trounced as Democrats swept to the House majority, leaving Johnson without a path to power.

The powerful speaker's gavel now is expected to pass to Democrats, who are preparing to nominate House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York for the job, second in line to the president. The House speaker's election is among the first votes of the new Congress, on Jan. 3, 2027.

Johnson first won the speaker's gavel in 2023 after his colleagues ousted the previous GOP speaker, Kevin McCarthy of California, in a first-of-its-kind coup in House history.

A lower-level member of House leadership, Johnson in many ways fell into the job after Republican colleagues could not agree on a next-in-line successor to McCarthy. He had distinguished himself before the Jan. 6, 2021 attack on the Capitol by organizing support for Trump's false claims of widespread fraud in the 2020 election he lost to Democrat Joe Biden.

Once in office, Johnson quickly pulled closer to Trump — so close that Johnson candidly recounts their almost daily phone calls and chats, often offering his impressions in the president's voice.

Johnson led passage of the GOP's signature package of tax breaks and social services cuts that Trump signed into law. He protected the president and his administration from embarrassing votes, including a recent effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, by simply sending lawmakers home.

Johnson's decision sets up a potential repeat of the leadership battles that have played out in recent years between the House GOP's conservative and far-right flanks.

Scalise, the majority leader, has long courted backing from the House GOP's conservative wing, particularly business and energy sector lawmakers. Jordan, the brawling former wrestler who helmed the Judiciary Committee, has long been preferred by the hard right, including some from the Freedom Caucus.

Both Scalise and Jordan reached for the speaker's gavel once McCarthy was forced aside in 2023, but they failed to win majority support from their colleagues, splitting the votes. At the time, Johnson emerged as the consensus candidate who became the House speaker.

articles.title: Stephen A. Smith issues a warning to Democrats on midterm wins
articles.summary: Democrats now have control of both chambers of Congress. And that means the question of whether they’ll try to impeach President Donald Trump for a third tim...
articles.body:
Democrats now have control of both chambers of Congress. And that means the question of whether they'll try to impeach President Donald Trump for a third time is no longer hypothetical. But ESPN star Stephen A. Smith does not think that would be wise.

Over the past several months, Smith has become more outspoken about his political views and even teased the possibility of running for office himself in 2028. But before a single vote was cast, he had a warning for the party as he made it clear that he thinks impeaching Trump would be a massive mistake.

On an episode of his Straight Shooter podcast released ahead of the midterms , Smith said that he's all for checks and balances. But he didn't think impeachment was the answer.

"But when people want the Democrats to regain the House so they can impeach the president, we really going to go through that again? The man was convicted of 34 felony counts. He was impeached not once but twice. He's still a president," Smith said.

Smith argued that impeachment isn't what voters want to see.

"You really think that it's good for this country if the Democrats regain office before the 2028 election to pursue this man and to try to impeach him? You really, really think that America wants that nonsense again? This is the kind of stuff that makes you look at the Democratic Party and say, 'Yo, see, that's why y'all turn people off.' No one is sitting here absolving Trump from a damn thing," Smith said.

He argued that Americans care far more about the cost of living.

"They want the gas prices to come down. They want the price of groceries to come down. They want interest rates to be reasonable. They want to be able to afford their groceries. They want to be able to afford gas. They want to be able to afford to pay their rent and their mortgages. That's what they want to do," Smith said.

In fact, Smith went as far as to warn Democrats that impeaching Trump would guarantee that a Republican would win the presidency in 2028.

"I'm going to make a prediction right here and now for everybody to see and everybody to hear after the Democrats reclaim the House this Tuesday, assuming they hold on to the Senate," Smith said. "If the Democrats pursue impeachment against Trump, I'm guaranteeing that a Republican will win the presidency in 2028. You can book it."

Smith made it clear that his warning wasn't a defense of Trump. He called Trump's comments about Venezuela and Iran "awful" and said he never approved of how ICE has operated.

"My point is I don't give a damn what he just said. Don't waste your time impeaching him. Govern the country. Show that you want to govern. Show that you're thinking about the American people instead of yourself, your vitriol, and your own commitment to vengeance," Smith said.

"Otherwise, you can win back the House this Tuesday all you want, Democratic Party. You ain't going to win the presidency in 2028," he added.

Smith got the House right, but he missed on the Senate. He predicted that "Republicans are going to hold on to the Senate." Instead, Democrats won the chamber decisively, winning nearly every battleground state to give them full control of Congress.

That takes away one of the biggest obstacles to impeachment. Removing a president still requires a two-thirds vote in the Senate, however, so a conviction would remain a long shot.

Trump himself has been bracing for this. In January, he told House Republicans at a retreat that if they lost the midterms, " I'll be impeached ."

Whether Democrats take Smith's advice remains to be seen.
